false_positives.candidate:
Test named reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey actually only disables realm passkeys

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(FALSE)`, i.e. it verifies that the passkey form is hidden when the realm does not have passkeys enabled — not that it is hidden for a user who has no passkey credential. Since `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` only checks the realm/feature flag and never whether the user owns a WebAuthn credential, a passkeys-enabled realm will now render the passkey option during re-authentication for users with no (or no discoverable) passkey, and `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators()` returns false so no `allowCredentials` is sent, making the option unusable for such users. There is no test covering that combination, and the misleading test name hides the gap.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative slice on a QuerySet raises ValueError, not supported by Django

In the `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch, `start_offset` (and often `stop`) are negative and used as `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice bounds, so the comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Since `offset` comes straight from the user-supplied `cursor` query parameter (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative integers), any authorized caller can trigger an unhandled 500 by sending e.g. `cursor=0:-1:0` with `optimized_pagination=true`. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member can be None -> AttributeError 500

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally when the requester is not a superuser. For requests authenticated with an org API key/auth token (or any caller that passes `OrganizationAuditPermission` without being a member), `member` is `None`, so this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'` and the endpoint returns a 500 for every GET, not just optimized ones. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None` and only evaluate the flag when `use_optimized` is actually requested.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime keys

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on the raw attribute value, which only works for numeric keys. The only caller (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. `build_cursor()` always invokes `key=self.get_item_key` on the results, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row will 500. The class should subclass/reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key handling (or at minimum not be wired to a datetime-ordered queryset).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
"admin-only" gate is actually satisfied by any member of an open-membership org

The comment says the optimized path is enabled only for "authorized administrators", but the condition uses `member.has_global_access`, which is true for every member of an organization with open membership (and for any member whose role grants global access), not just admins/owners. Combined with the new unvalidated negative-offset path in `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, this lets ordinary members reach code that bypasses the normal offset bounds and crashes the request. If this is meant to be admin-only, check the actual role/permission (e.g. superuser or `org:admin`); the claim that "permissions are checked at the queryset level" in paginator.py is also unsupported for this path.

Extra-row trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice offset

The check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` compares the number of fetched rows against the un-clamped `offset`, but the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which can differ from `offset` after clamping or in the negative-offset branch). When they differ, the extra look-ahead row is not dropped, so a previous-page response can contain `limit + 1` items / an item that belongs to the adjacent page. Use `start_offset` consistently (same issue exists in the `BasePaginator` copy at line 192).

Misleading comment documents negative offsets as a supported feature

The added comment states that `Cursor` now "allows negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no behavior changed here (offsets were never validated) and downstream consumers cannot handle negative offsets: Django querysets reject negative slice bounds and `OffsetPaginator`/`ChainPaginator` explicitly raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Documenting an unsupported, user-controllable value as a feature invites more code to rely on it; either add real validation here or drop the comment.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` endpoint branch are added with no unit or API tests. Given that the class as written raises `TypeError` on datetime keys and `ValueError` on negative slices, even a single test exercising the new query parameter would have caught the breakage. Tests should cover: optimized path with/without a cursor, negative offsets, and unauthorized callers falling back to `DateTimePaginator`.

Silently clamping negative offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes `BasePaginator.get_result()` for every paginator in the codebase: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced an error, now silently returns the first page as if the cursor were `offset=0`, while the cursors returned in the response are built from the original negative `cursor.offset` (see `_build_next_values`/`_build_prev_values`), producing inconsistent/incorrect next/prev links. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed through and will raise Django's `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` (a 500) rather than a `BadPaginationError`. Negative offsets should be validated and rejected explicitly in one place.

value_from_cursor returns raw int for a datetime column

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor()` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (integer/float), but `BasePaginator.build_queryset()` injects it into a raw SQL `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` clause. Since the endpoint orders by `-datetime`, the value must be converted back to a `datetime` as `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor()` does. As written, following any cursor will either raise a database type error or silently compare a timestamp column against an integer, returning wrong pages. Additionally, cursor values produced by `DateTimePaginator` (milliseconds) and this paginator are not interchangeable, so a client toggling `optimized_pagination` between requests will feed incompatible cursors to the other paginator.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative slice start on a Django QuerySet raises ValueError, not "handled automatically"

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django explicitly rejects this: `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. Since `Cursor.from_string` happily parses a negative offset from the user-supplied `cursor` query parameter, a request like `?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-5:0` produces an unhandled exception / 500 rather than a 400. The inline comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` like `OffsetPaginator` does.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is numeric-keyed but is used with the `datetime` column

The endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and whose `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor integer. `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and a cursor value would be compared against a timestamp column as a bare integer in the generated `WHERE` clause. Any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an authorized user will therefore fail with a 500 instead of returning a page. Date-keyed querysets require `DateTimePaginator`-style key handling (the `multiplier` conversion).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator now silently clamps negative cursor offsets, producing inconsistent cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the behavior of every paginator derived from `BasePaginator` (issues, audit logs, many list endpoints). Previously a negative offset in a client-supplied cursor surfaced as an error from the ORM; now the query silently starts at row 0 while `build_cursor` is still handed the original negative `cursor.offset`. `_build_next_values` then computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the negative value and `_build_prev_values` treats the negative offset as "has_prev", so the returned next/prev cursors point at positions that do not correspond to the rows actually returned, causing skipped or duplicated rows on subsequent pages. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly rather than clamped.

Eviction silently drops spans with a hardcoded limit and no metric/log

`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` trims segments to a hardcoded 1000 spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured value and is no longer used anywhere, so the setting has no effect and the two numbers disagree; (2) the previous code path in `_load_segment_data` that dropped oversized segments emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and `logger.error`, and that observability was removed in this PR. Now span data is discarded with no metric, log, or configuration, making truncated segments undetectable in production.

Misleading comment claims a behavior change that was not made

The added comment says "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no code changed here — `Cursor` always accepted negative offsets, and callers (e.g. `OffsetPaginator`) are the ones that validate them. The comment implies `Cursor` now intentionally supports negative offsets as a feature, which will mislead future readers into assuming downstream paginators handle them safely (they do not; Django rejects negative slice starts).

Module docstring still describes Redis sets after the switch to sorted sets

The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`) scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted at insert time when a segment exceeds the limit. The docstring (step 3 "Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`" and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes plain sets and says nothing about scoring or eviction, so readers will have the wrong mental model of the key types and of the fact that spans can be dropped.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new public paginator with non-trivial branching (negative-offset path, prev-cursor extra-row trimming, `enable_advanced_features` flag) and it is already wired into a production endpoint, yet no tests are added for it or for the audit-log endpoint's new `optimized_pagination` code path. The datetime/negative-slice failures in this class would have been caught by a single test.

No test for the new insert-time eviction behavior

The headline change of this PR is eviction during insert (`zpopmin` once a segment exceeds 1000 spans) plus the set→sorted-set migration, but no test exercises a segment larger than the limit. Existing tests only cover 4-5 span segments, so neither the trimming threshold, the choice of which spans are discarded (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`), nor the removal of the old `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data` is verified. A regression in the Lua arithmetic (e.g. off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`, or the `span_count == 0` fallback) would go unnoticed.

Prev-page trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice start

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the extra-row trim condition `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` uses the raw `cursor.offset`, while the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which may differ, e.g. clamped to 0 or negative). When `offset` is negative the comparison can never be true (or is true for the wrong row count), so the extra look-behind row fetched for `is_prev` cursors is not dropped and leaks into the returned page, duplicating a row the client already saw. The condition should compare against `start_offset + limit + extra`.

Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced 10x reduction in the maximum redirect-chain depth: traces whose parent/child redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to the correct `set_key`, so their spans get split across multiple segments and are emitted as separate (incorrect) segments. If the reduction is intentional it should be stated in the PR and the caveat comment kept; otherwise the original bound should be restored.

`max_segment_spans` is now dead configuration

The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere; the effective limit is the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua`. Callers that set this parameter will silently get no behavior change. Either wire the value through to the Lua script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

`organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the requester is not an organization member (e.g. org auth token / integration token auth, or a staff/superuser request that resolves no membership). Because `request.user.is_superuser` is `False` for non-user auth (and `AnonymousUser`), the second operand is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a 500 for those auth paths. The flag should only be computed inside the `optimized_pagination` branch and must null-check `member`.

zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting span timestamps/scores

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. The scores are `end_timestamp_precise` values used to order spans for eviction. If the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a redelivered/duplicated span that landed under a different key before the redirect was established), its score becomes the sum of two ~1.7e9 timestamps, making it the newest member forever and causing `zpopmin` to evict legitimate newer spans instead. The merges should specify `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) to preserve timestamp semantics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key built from Python `hash()` of project ids can collide

The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Using an opaque 64-bit hash instead of the sorted ids themselves means two different project sets in the same organization can map to the same key, in which case one set inherits the other's eligibility verdict and the returned counts are silently wrong (either inflated or not upsampled). Since this cache is shared across processes, the wrong value is served broadly. Serialize the sorted ids (or a stable digest with low collision risk) into the key instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `discover` for the errors-only/transactions-only probe queries) while the outer `dataset` is still the originally requested one (e.g. `metrics_enhanced_performance`). As a result the upsampling decision is computed for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling is silently skipped for the split errors query (under-reported counts for allowlisted projects) and could conversely be applied to a dataset whose query builder has no `upsampled_count` function. The check should use `scoped_dataset`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
60s eligibility cache has no working invalidation; option changes are ignored and the cache adds little value

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds keyed by org + project ids. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to clear it but is never called from anywhere in the codebase, and it requires knowing the exact project-id set used in the cache key, so it cannot realistically invalidate all affected entries when `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes. Consequence: adding or (more importantly) removing a project from the allowlist — e.g. to stop emitting inflated counts during an incident — takes effect only after up to 60s, with no way to force it. Note also that `options.get` is already backed by the options cache, so the extra caching layer buys little while introducing this staleness and a stale-data risk. The surrounding docstring claiming "we always have the latest configuration state" contradicts the caching behaviour.

Error-focus detection reads `request.GET['query']` instead of the query actually executed

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` / `_is_error_focused_query` inspect the raw `request.GET["query"]`, but `_get_event_stats` is frequently called with a *modified* query string: the dashboard widget split path builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (errors-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transactions-only). Because the helper never sees these, the errors-only probe query is not recognized as error-focused (upsampling skipped, counts under-reported) while the transactions-only query inherits the decision made from the original request. The query string that is actually executed should be passed into the helper.

Misleading comments on upsampled count assertions

`assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` (and the following line) claim the bucket contains 1 event while asserting a count of 10. The value 10 is the upsampled count (1 event at a 0.1 client sample rate); the comment makes the assertion look wrong and will mislead the next person debugging a failure here. State that the raw event count is 1 and the expected upsampled count is 10.

Stray git submodule entry `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`) at path `sentry-repo` with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local tooling: it pollutes the repository tree, makes `git submodule status/update` and some clone/CI tooling report errors for an unregistered submodule, and pins a commit of the repository inside itself. It should be removed from the PR.

Test factory fabricates `sample_rate` and silently swallows all errors

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` injects `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` from `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` in `store_event`, bypassing the real ingest path (relay/event manager) that is responsible for deriving the sampling weight in production. The new endpoint tests therefore validate upsampled counts against a value the test harness itself invents, so a regression in the real normalization/ingest logic would not be caught. Additionally both `try/except Exception: pass` blocks hide genuine problems (e.g. a non-numeric `client_sample_rate`), silently producing events without a sample rate and turning a meaningful assertion failure into a confusing count mismatch.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated error queries

`_is_error_focused_query` does `"event.type:error" in query`. This matches `!event.type:error` (a query that explicitly excludes errors, i.e. transactions) as well as occurrences inside quoted free-text/message filters. For such queries the discover `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (`sum(sample_weight)`), producing wrong (or null/zero) numbers for non-error rows where `sample_weight` is absent. The check needs to parse the query (or at least exclude negations) rather than do a raw substring test.

`setUp` overwrites `self.user` after `login_as`, and no coverage for errors dataset / caching

In the new `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user after `self.login_as(user=self.user)`, so `self.user` no longer refers to the authenticated user; any later use of `self.user` for auth assertions in this class would be wrong (the workaround `self.authed_user` hints at the confusion). The class also lacks tests for the two riskiest new behaviours: requests with `dataset=errors` (where `upsampled_count()` is applied unconditionally) and the newly added 60-second eligibility cache (stale allowlist results), both of which are currently unverified.

`toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` can yield NULL and is exposed as a public function

Two problems with the new `upsampled_count` SnQL function: (1) `sample_weight` is not guaranteed to be populated for all error rows in an allowlisted project (events ingested before the feature was enabled, or SDKs not sending `contexts.error_sampling`); for a nullable column ClickHouse `sum` over all-NULL rows returns NULL, and `toInt64` of that stays NULL, so the timeseries can return `null` counts where consumers (zerofill, frontend charts, alert comparisons) expect integers. The docstring's assumption that "sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects" is not enforced anywhere — consider `ifNull(...)`/`sumIf` semantics. (2) Unlike the neighbouring internal helpers, it is not marked `private=True`, so any user can request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover for non-allowlisted projects and get meaningless zero/null results, a new public API surface that was presumably not intended.

`upsampled_count()` only registered for the discover dataset, but applied to the errors dataset

`upsampled_count` is added only to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter`, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` returns `True` unconditionally when `dataset is sentry.snuba.errors`. The errors dataset is resolved through its own `ErrorsDatasetConfig` function registry, which does not contain `upsampled_count`, so any `yAxis=count()` request with `dataset=errors` for allowlisted projects will be rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` and then fail with an "is not a valid function" search error instead of returning data. There is also no test exercising `dataset=errors`, so this path is completely uncovered.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs error ids with nodestore values by dict ordering

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi()` returns a dict whose iteration order exactly matches the order of the `node_ids` passed in and contains an entry for every id. That is an implementation detail of the backend; if any backend omits missing keys or returns a differently ordered mapping, each `ErrorEvent.id` will be attached to another error's title/message/timestamp. Build the list by iterating the input ids and looking up `events[Event.generate_node_id(project_id, id)]` instead of relying on value ordering.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New table widget renders hardcoded empty data when feature flag is on

In `tableResultComponent`, when `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of the actual `result`/`fields`/`meta` computed just above. Any organization that gets this flag will see completely blank dashboard tables instead of their widget data. The real result must be mapped into `TabularData`/`TabularColumn` before this branch can be enabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble")` gate and before any payload validation, so every request — including ones that are immediately rejected with 404 because the feature is disabled — is counted as an assemble event. This inflates the metric and makes it useless for measuring actual usage; move the call after the feature check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

false_positives.candidate:
60s processing deadline may be too short for a 100-identity batch and breaks the task chain

`check_auth_identities` iterates up to `chunk_size` (default 100) identities and calls `provider.refresh_identity()` for each, which performs an external HTTP round trip per identity. With `processing_deadline_duration=60` the worker will kill the task once the deadline passes; because `check_auth.apply_async(...)` is only executed at the very end of the function, a deadline kill also drops the self-rescheduling call, halting the chained scan of remaining identities until the next scheduled run. Either reduce the chunk size or set a deadline that bounds 100 sequential network calls.

Error and replay-event timestamps are compared in different units

`gen_request_data` interleaves error messages with replay breadcrumbs by comparing `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"]` against `event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from the nodestore event payload and is epoch **seconds** (~1.7e9), while rrweb replay events carry epoch **milliseconds** (~1.75e12). Every error therefore compares as smaller than every replay event, so in production all errors will be flushed to the front of the log list instead of being placed chronologically, which is the whole point of the merge. The new unit test (`test_get_request_data`) uses second-scale timestamps for the replay events too, so it cannot catch this; a test with realistic millisecond rrweb timestamps is needed.

Serializer accepts reports with neither `timestamp` nor `age`

`age` and `timestamp` are both declared `required=False` and the `validate_age`/`validate_timestamp` hooks only reject the case where *both* are present. A report containing neither field passes validation even though both the Working Draft and Editor's Draft require one of them, so malformed payloads are silently accepted and counted. A `validate()` method asserting exactly one of the two is present would close the gap (and there is no test covering this case).

TabularColumn.name is typed as the field-key generic instead of string

`TabularColumn<TFields>` declares `name: TFields`, the same type as `key`. `name` is a human-readable display label (the new table explicitly supports custom names such as 'Count of Span Duration'), so once a caller instantiates `TabularColumn<'http.request_method' | 'count(span.duration)'>` the display name becomes impossible to set without a cast. `name` should be `string`.

`Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always true, so the guard is dead

`normalizeDateTimeParams(selection.datetime)` always returns an object (possibly empty), so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` can never be false and the `enabled` condition reduces to the feature check alone. If the intent was to avoid firing the request before page filters are ready (e.g. checking for a statsPeriod/start+end), the condition needs to inspect the actual fields; as written it provides no protection and will issue a request with no date range.

get_environment_info issues an extra event lookup per issue and swallows errors as 'no-environment'

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (a Snuba/eventstore lookup) plus `get_environment()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment, i.e. up to 5 extra queries per comment on top of the existing top-issues query. In addition, the blanket `except Exception` logs `get_environment_info.no-environment` with `extra={"error": e}`, which both mislabels real failures (timeouts, Snuba errors) as 'no environment' and loses the traceback (no `exc_info`/`logger.exception`), making such failures effectively invisible.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The code decrypts `user.backupCodes`, nulls the matched entry in memory and writes the whole re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both read the array before either writes, so the same single-use code is accepted twice. Likewise, two concurrent logins using two different codes will each write back their own copy of the array, and the last write resurrects the code consumed by the other request. Consuming the code should be done atomically (e.g. inside a transaction with a conditional update / row lock) so a code can be redeemed exactly once.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
"missing_backup_codes" message points to a settings flow that does not exist

The new string `missing_backup_codes` says "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." but there is no UI anywhere in this PR to generate or regenerate backup codes: codes are only created inside `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup`, which rejects users who already have 2FA enabled (`TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled`). Every user who enabled 2FA before this change (and any user who closed the dialog without saving the codes) will hit this error and will be told to do something that is impossible without first disabling 2FA. Either add a regeneration endpoint/UI or change the message to tell the user to disable and re-enable 2FA.

Assertion on the 2FA switch is a no-op and is left unfixed

`expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the unawaited Promise returned by `isChecked()`, which is always truthy, so the first test never verifies that 2FA was actually enabled (the PR adds a FIXME acknowledging this instead of fixing it). With the new backup-codes step inserted into the flow this assertion is the only post-enable check in that test, so a regression in the enable flow would not be caught. Use `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()` or the `[data-state="checked"]` locator as the second test does.

Backup-code branch allows login without password verification

In `authorize()` the password is only verified when `credentials.totpCode` is empty (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` at line 121). The new backup-code branch at line 131 is evaluated for `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` regardless of whether a password was checked, and it takes precedence over the TOTP branch. A request that sends any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") together with a valid `backupCode` therefore skips password verification entirely and also never validates the TOTP code, so the backup code alone grants a session. Backup codes are meant to be a second factor (they are even downloaded to a plain text file / copied to the clipboard), so this turns a leaked backup code into a full account takeover. The backup-code path should require successful password verification before accepting the code.

Dismissing the backup-codes dialog skips onEnable(), leaving the parent UI stale

2FA is already enabled on the server when the `DisplayBackupCodes` step is shown, but `onEnable()` is only called by the "Close" button. If the user dismisses the dialog with the X / Escape / overlay (which goes through `onOpenChange`), the parent's enable callback never runs, so the two-factor switch and any cached profile data keep showing 2FA as disabled until a reload, and the user loses the codes without any warning. The enable callback should also run when the dialog is closed from this step.

No test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The core new behaviour of this PR — authenticating with a backup code in `next-auth-options.ts` (including single-use consumption) and in the disable endpoint — has no automated coverage; the added test only clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the new dialog and the file notes this as a TODO. Regressions such as a code being reusable, or the "Lost access" flow sending the wrong field, would go undetected.

Unvalidated backupCode body field can crash the endpoint

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes the field is a string. A client sending a non-string JSON value (number, array, object) makes the handler throw a TypeError, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 instead of a 400 validation error. The same pattern exists for `credentials.backupCode` in next-auth-options.ts. The field should be validated (type and expected format) before use. Also note `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` is unguarded and will throw a 500 if the stored value cannot be decrypted/parsed.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TypeError when evt.destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` whenever the event has no destination calendar (now a common case: handleNewBooking sets `destinationCalendar: null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has one). The very next line dereferences it unconditionally: `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` and aborts `EventManager.create()` for any Google Meet booking made by a user without a destination calendar. Use optional chaining (`mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent fallback calendar lookup can never match

`event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is only evaluated when `externalCalendarId` is falsy (the ternary's else branch), so it compares each `cal.externalId` against `undefined`/`""` and always returns `undefined`. The previous code used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Consequently, when no external calendar id is passed, `calendar.events.update({ calendarId: undefined })` is issued instead of targeting the destination calendar, and the update fails. The intent was presumably to fall back to the first (main host) destination calendar.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Organization slug assignment logic inverted

`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` inverts the previous condition `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`. The intent is: when billing is enabled the slug is only *requested* (stored in `metadata.requestedSlug` until payment), otherwise the slug is set directly. With this change, a billing-enabled instance sets both `slug` and `metadata.requestedSlug`, and a non-billing instance (self-hosted) creates the organization with **no slug at all**, so org subdomain resolution/`orgDomains` lookups break for newly created orgs. This change is also unrelated to the PR's stated purpose.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Calendar.createEvent credentialId made a required parameter

`createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number)` adds a required second parameter to the public `Calendar` interface. Any caller outside of `CalendarManager` (other packages/apps, third-party calendar app implementations in the app store that are invoked directly) that calls `createEvent(evt)` now fails type-checking, and at runtime receives `undefined` for `credentialId` — which in GoogleCalendarService makes the destination-calendar lookup fail and silently writes to `primary`. Making the parameter optional and defensively handling `undefined` would avoid both the contract break and the silent misrouting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Collective team destination calendars silently dropped when organizer has none

`evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` uses optional chaining, and `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. In that case all the collected host destination calendars are discarded, so collective hosts get no calendar invite — exactly the scenario this PR aims to fix. Initialize the array (e.g. `[]`) before pushing, or build the array in one expression.

Duplicate calendar events created for multiple destination calendars without credentialId

For each destination with no `credentialId`, the code filters *all* of the organizer's credentials of that integration type and creates an event with each. With the new multi-destination array (e.g. two collective hosts both having a Google destination calendar with `credentialId: null`), this loop runs once per destination using the same credential set, producing N duplicate events in the same calendar. The per-destination branch should create at most one event for the destination it is iterating over.

Dynamic-booking user select no longer fetches organization slug

The rewritten `loadUsers` dropped `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the `prisma.user.findMany` select used for dynamic (no eventTypeId) bookings. This field was added deliberately for org-aware booker URLs; without it any downstream use of `user.organization?.slug` resolves to undefined (or fails type-checking because the two branches of `loadUsers` now return different shapes), producing wrong links for dynamic group bookings in organizations. The removal is unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor.

Empty dynamicUserList surfaces as a 500 instead of a 400

`throw new Error("dynamicUserList is not properly defined or empty.")` is a plain `Error`, so the catch below (which only re-wraps `HttpError` and Prisma errors as 400) converts it into `HttpError({ statusCode: 500, message: "Unable to load users" })`. A malformed/empty client-supplied user list is a client error and previously did not produce a 5xx; this will pollute error monitoring and give the booker no useful message.

Hangout-link patch sends calendarId: undefined

In `createEvent`, the follow-up `calendar.events.patch({ calendarId: selectedCalendar, ... })` uses `selectedCalendar` directly, but `selectedCalendar` can now be `undefined` (the `|| "primary"` default was moved to the insert call only). When the destination calendar can't be resolved, the insert succeeds against `primary` while the patch that adds the Meet link to the description is sent with no calendarId and fails.

Recurring-cancellation deletion repeated once per calendar reference

The recurring + `allRemainingBookings` block (which itself loops over every user calendar credential and every updated booking) is now nested inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With multiple calendar references (the normal case for the new multi-host destination calendars) the same delete calls are issued refs × credentials × bookings times, multiplying external API calls against Google/Office and relying on 404/410 swallowing for correctness. The recurring branch should run once, outside the per-reference loop.

Video booking references no longer store credentialId

`credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined` drops the credentialId for non-calendar (video) results; the previous code used `result.credentialId` in that branch. Video meeting references are therefore persisted with `credentialId: null`. Cancellation logic depends on it: `handleCancelBooking` only deletes the meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is truthy (see packages/features/bookings/lib/handleCancelBooking.ts ~line 491), so Zoom/MS Teams/etc. meetings will silently stop being deleted when a booking is cancelled.

Webhook payload destinationCalendar shape is now inconsistent (null vs []) and breaking for consumers

`destinationCalendar` in the webhook payload changes from an object/null to an array, but the code paths are inconsistent: BOOKING_REJECTED/confirm now emits `[]` (this assertion), while BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED still assert `null` (lines 119 and 373) because handleNewBooking sets `null` when there is no destination calendar. External webhook consumers parsing `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` will break, and they now have to handle three shapes (object-less array, empty array, null). The shape should be normalized (always an array) and the payload change documented as breaking.

createEvent ignores destination calendars that have no credentialId

`selectedCalendar` is now resolved only by `cal.credentialId === credentialId`. `DestinationCalendar.credentialId` is nullable, and `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` explicitly handles that case by calling `createEvent(credential, event)` without an externalId. For those rows the `find` returns `undefined` and the event is created in `"primary"` instead of the user's configured destination calendar — a regression from the previous `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. A fallback to the destination calendar matching this integration (or the first one) is needed.

deleteEvent fallback calendar lookup can never match

Same self-defeating condition as in `updateEvent`: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it always resolves to `undefined` and the code silently falls back to `"primary"`. Previously it used `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Events stored in a non-primary destination calendar will therefore not be found/deleted (Google returns 404, which the handler swallows), leaving orphaned calendar events after cancellations.

updateAllCalendarEvents error message computed but never logged

The catch block still builds the diagnostic `message` (including credential type, userId and bookingId) but the `console.error(message)` call was removed in this change. Calendar update failures are now swallowed entirely with no log output, making production debugging of failed reschedules/updates impossible.

updateLocation creates booking references without externalCalendarId/credentialId

`externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId ?? undefined` are read from the results of `updateAllCalendarEvents`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` (packages/core/CalendarManager.ts:313-323) does not return `externalId` or `credentialId` at all — only `createEvent` was changed to return them. Previously these values came from `evt.destinationCalendar`. As a result, every booking reference created by an "edit location" action loses its calendar linkage, and subsequent updates/cancellations can no longer resolve the right credential/calendar (they fall back to iterating all credentials or to "primary").

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Injecting the literal string "refresh_token" overwrites valid stored refresh tokens

When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Several callers spread the parsed data over the existing credential key and persist it, e.g. `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` and writes it to the DB. Microsoft legitimately omits `refresh_token` on some refresh responses (the schema marks it optional), so the user's real refresh token is replaced in the database by the useless string "refresh_token" and the integration breaks permanently until re-installed. The same happens for zoomvideo, where `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` is persisted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema is built with bogus computed keys and strips every field except access_token

The schema is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. The computed keys evaluate `ZodString.toString()` / `ZodOptional.toString()`, which both produce the same literal string (`"[object Object]"`), so the resulting schema is just `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown? }`. The intended behaviour ("assume any property with a number is the expiry" and "allow other properties") is not implemented at all. Worse, because `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, parsing a credential-sync response discards `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token`, so callers that merge `tokenResponse.data` into the stored key (office365calendar, zoomvideo) end up with no expiry at all — the token is treated as permanently expired and refreshed on every request, and zoom computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + NaN`.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google credential key is overwritten with the zod safeParse wrapper object

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)`, i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, but the result is assigned to `key` and written straight to the DB (`prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`). Previously the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the credential object itself). After the first token refresh every Google Calendar credential will be stored as `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, which no longer satisfies `googleCredentialSchema`, so subsequent constructions of GoogleCalendarService throw and the calendar connection is broken for the user.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential-sync branch returns a fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific shapes

In the sync branch the helper returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, but the wrapped `refreshFunction` of most callers returns something completely different: google returns a Gaxios response (caller reads `res.data.access_token`), hubspot returns a parsed `HubspotToken` (caller reads `.expiresIn` and stores the object as the credential key), zoho-bigin and zohocrm return an axios response (callers read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token`). With app-credential syncing enabled these callers will read `undefined` off the `Response`, throw TypeErrors, compute `NaN` expiry dates, or persist a serialized `Response` as the credential key. The helper must normalise the sync response (await `response.json()`) into the same shape the refresh function returns, or each caller must be adapted.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
