Credential-sync branch returns a fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific shapes

In the sync branch the helper returns the raw `fetch` `Response`, but the wrapped `refreshFunction` of most callers returns something completely different: google returns a Gaxios response (caller reads `res.data.access_token`), hubspot returns a parsed `HubspotToken` (caller reads `.expiresIn` and stores the object as the credential key), zoho-bigin and zohocrm return an axios response (callers read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token`). With app-credential syncing enabled these callers will read `undefined` off the `Response`, throw TypeErrors, compute `NaN` expiry dates, or persist a serialized `Response` as the credential key. The helper must normalise the sync response (await `response.json()`) into the same shape the refresh function returns, or each caller must be adapted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zoho Bigin passes a credential id where a user id is expected

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes `credentialId` as the third argument, which the helper uses as `calcomUserId` in the credential-sync request body. The self-hosted endpoint will receive a credential id instead of the Cal.com user id, so it will either return the wrong user's tokens or fail. `refreshAccessToken` should receive and forward `credential.userId`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error detection via `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable

The refresh result is validated with `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw ...`. `statusText` is an empty string for HTTP/2 responses (undici does not synthesize a reason phrase), so a perfectly successful refresh can be rejected with an `HttpError` whose message is empty, while a non-2xx response with reason phrase "OK" would be accepted. Use `response.ok` / `response.status` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce connection still uses the old access token after refreshing

`getClient` now performs a refresh_token exchange and persists the new token, but the `jsforce.Connection` is still created with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the stale value read from the credential before refreshing) and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url`. The refresh is therefore pointless: if the stored access token was expired, every Salesforce API call still fails. The newly parsed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` / `instance_url` should be used.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook handler has no method guard and throws raw errors on malformed input

The handler accepts any HTTP verb (GET/DELETE included) and uses `schema.parse(req.body)` plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without try/catch. A malformed body, a payload encrypted with the wrong key, or non-JSON plaintext results in an unhandled exception and a 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400/422 with a useful message. Restrict to POST and use `safeParse` / wrap the decryption in a try/catch.

false_positives.candidate:
Credential-sync request is unauthenticated and its status is never checked

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret/signature header (unlike the inbound webhook, which verifies `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), so the self-hoster's endpoint has no way to tell that the request really came from Cal.com — anybody who knows the URL can harvest access tokens for arbitrary user ids if the endpoint trusts the caller. In addition the response status is never checked, so a 4xx/5xx body is passed to the token parsers as if it were a token response, producing confusing downstream failures instead of a clear error.

No tests for the new credential webhook or the token-parsing helpers

This PR adds a publicly reachable endpoint that decrypts a payload and writes third-party OAuth credentials for arbitrary user ids, plus two new shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) used by ~10 app integrations, with no unit tests. Basic tests covering secret mismatch, unknown user/app, bad ciphertext, create-vs-update behaviour, and the token-schema fallback would have caught the schema and response-shape defects noted elsewhere in this review.

Salesforce token is refreshed unconditionally on every service instantiation

`getClient` issues a refresh_token request to `login.salesforce.com` and a `credential.update` write every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, with no expiry check on the stored token. Since the service is constructed per booking/availability operation this adds a blocking round trip plus a DB write to every request and will hit Salesforce's refresh-token rate limits on busy instances.

Updating synced credentials does not clear the `invalid` flag

When a credential already exists the handler only writes `key`. Credentials that were previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. google/zoom/webex set this on `invalid_grant`) stay invalid after fresh keys are pushed in, so Cal.com keeps treating the connection as broken even though valid tokens were just synced. The update should also reset `invalid: false`.

Webex refresh still validated with the strict provider schema, so credential sync cannot work

Webex was switched to `refreshOAuthTokens` but the response is still validated with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(...)`, which requires an exact `scope` literal, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A self-hosted sync endpoint is documented to return only the access token and expiry, so the parse always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here (as done for zoom/office365) or don't wire Webex into the sync flow.

Webhook secret compared with a non-constant-time `!==` and header may be an array

The shared secret check uses a plain string inequality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is therefore vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally `req.headers[name]` can be `string[]` when the header is sent twice, in which case the comparison always fails and legitimate callers get a 403 with no explanation.

Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo", which is not the app's slug

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug used everywhere else (callback stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint looks the app up with `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`) is `zoom`. A self-hoster keying off `appSlug` will not be able to map the sync request back to the credential the webhook created, so Zoom credential syncing silently fails.

`prisma` is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService

The newly added code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` inside `getClient`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile error (and a `ReferenceError` at runtime if type-checking is bypassed), so every Salesforce booking/calendar operation fails as soon as the service is instantiated.

findFirst + update can leave duplicate credentials out of sync

Because the lookup is `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })`, when a user has more than one credential row for the same app (which happens for several apps that historically allowed duplicates) only one row is updated; the stale rows keep their old keys and may still be selected by other code paths (`findFirst` is used in several adapters). Two concurrent webhook deliveries can also both see no credential and create two rows. Consider a unique constraint or an `updateMany`/transaction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist and duplicate checks are case-sensitive, allowing bypass and duplicate attendees

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is lower-cased but the incoming `guest` string is not, so `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` can be trivially bypassed by submitting a different case (e.g. `Spam@Example.com`). The same case-sensitivity applies to the existing-attendee comparison `guest === attendee.email`, so the same address in a different case is inserted again, producing duplicate attendee rows and duplicate emails. Both comparisons should normalize case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team permission check uses AND instead of OR

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. A user is either an admin or an owner, never usually both in the sense these helpers test, so the expression is almost always false for a team admin and, despite the variable name, this does not grant admins access. The result is that team admins (and in many membership models owners too, if `isTeamAdmin` returns false for role OWNER) cannot add guests to their team's bookings even though the name/intent says they should. This should be `||`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails receives the raw input list instead of the actually-added guests

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the unfiltered input array. In `email-manager.ts` this list decides who receives the "you were invited" (`AttendeeScheduledEmail`) vs the "guests added" notice. Any email the caller submitted that was already an attendee (filtered out into `uniqueGuests`) will therefore receive a brand-new booking confirmation email again instead of the add-guests notification. `uniqueGuests` should be passed instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No limit or de-duplication on the guests array server-side

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no max length and no uniqueness constraint; the uniqueness/validity checks only exist client-side in `AddGuestsDialog`. Any authenticated user who is an attendee of a booking can POST hundreds of arbitrary addresses and the handler will create an attendee row and send a booking email to each one, turning the endpoint into an email-sending relay (spam/abuse vector) and bloating the booking's attendee list. Add a `.max(...)` bound and de-duplicate (case-insensitively) in the schema/handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event type disableStandardEmails settings

Unlike every other sender in this file (e.g. `sendLocationChangeEmails`), `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no `eventTypeMetadata` and never calls `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. Event types configured with `disableStandardEmails.all.host`/`.attendee` will still send host and attendee emails when guests are added, violating the user's explicit email-suppression setting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Email failure swallowed without the error details

`catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` discards `err`, so a mail delivery or template failure leaves no diagnosable trace. Use the project `logger` and include `safeStringify(err)` plus the booking id.

EventManager built from the caller's credentials, not the booking organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` fetches the credentials of the logged-in caller, and the EventManager is constructed with `{...user, credentials}`. Since this endpoint is reachable by attendees and team admins (not just the organizer), the calendar/video update in `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` will be attempted with credentials that do not own the external calendar event, so the attendee update silently fails (or targets the wrong account). The credentials and destination calendar should come from the booking's organizer (`booking.user`).

Invalid-email banner is never cleared and empty submit is a silent no-op

`setIsInvalidEmail(false)` is only called by the Cancel button; on a successful mutation (or when the user corrects the input) the flag stays true, so the red "Emails must be unique and valid" message is still displayed the next time the dialog is opened via the dropdown. Additionally, when the user removes all email rows, `handleAdd` returns early with no toast or message, so clicking "Add" appears to do nothing.

New UI component imports from its own package barrel, creating a cycle

`packages/ui/form/MultiEmail.tsx` imports `Button, EmailField, Icon, Tooltip` from `@calcom/ui`, while `packages/ui/index.tsx` re-exports this very module (via `MultiEmailLazy`). This self-referential cycle can resolve to `undefined` components at runtime depending on module evaluation order/bundler, producing "Element type is invalid" render errors. Import the components by relative path (as the sibling form components do) instead of through the package barrel.

No tests for the new addGuests mutation

The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that writes attendees and sends emails, with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer / attendee / team admin), blacklist filtering and duplicate filtering, but no unit or integration tests were added. Regressions in the permission branches would silently allow or deny guest additions; the AND/OR bug in the team check is exactly the kind of defect a test would have caught.

No validation of booking status or time before adding guests

The handler accepts any `bookingId` and never checks `booking.status` or whether the booking is in the past. The UI only exposes the action for upcoming/confirmed bookings, but the tRPC mutation is directly callable, so guests can be added to CANCELLED/REJECTED or long-past bookings, which then triggers confirmation/ics emails for an event that no longer exists. It also does not account for `seatsPerTimeSlot`: adding attendees to a seated event bypasses the seat limit and creates attendees with no seat reference.

Subject line dereferences attendees[0] without a guard

`name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw a TypeError if `calEvent.attendees` is empty, which would reject the whole `sendAddGuestsEmails` promise chain. Other organizer templates guard this; use optional access or fall back to the organizer/team name.

Team hosts never notified because the CalendarEvent has no team data

`sendAddGuestsEmails` loops over `calendarEvent.team?.members` to notify co-hosts, but the `evt` built in `addGuests.handler.ts` never populates `team` (the booking query selects `eventType` without team/hosts). For team events, only the primary organizer is emailed and the branch is dead code.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS reminders or to unscheduled rows

The new `OR` branch in the `deleteMany` matches **any** `WorkflowReminder` whose `retryCount > 1`, with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` and no `scheduled: false` constraint. Consequences: (1) the SMS cron will delete EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders as soon as some other code path (e.g. a future whatsapp/email cron reusing the same column) increments their retryCount, destroying reminders this endpoint is not responsible for; (2) a row that already has `scheduled: true` and a `referenceId` (a message really scheduled in Twilio) would also be deleted if its retryCount ever reached 2, leaving an orphaned scheduled Twilio message that can no longer be cancelled when the booking is cancelled/rescheduled. The branch should at minimum be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduled: false, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new retry/delete behaviour

The PR introduces a destructive rule (reminders are permanently deleted after two failed scheduling attempts) with no accompanying test. There is no coverage for: incrementing retryCount when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy, incrementing on thrown errors, and the deleteMany removing only rows that should be removed. Given that a wrong predicate silently deletes customer reminders, at least a unit test around the delete/where clause and the increment paths is warranted.

OR'ed deleteMany on unindexed retryCount forces a full table scan each cron run

`retryCount` has no index (see schema: only `[bookingUid]`, `[workflowStepId]`, `[seatReferenceId]`, `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]`, `[cancelled, scheduledDate]`). Wrapping the previous predicate in an `OR` with `retryCount > 1` means Postgres can no longer satisfy the delete with the `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` index alone and will likely sequentially scan `WorkflowReminder`, which is one of the largest tables, on every run of this cron. Either add an index covering the new predicate or keep the retry cleanup as a second, method-scoped `deleteMany` that can use the existing index.

Unguarded prisma.update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

In the `catch` block the `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` call is not itself wrapped in a try/catch. If the original error was caused by database unavailability (or the row was deleted concurrently, producing a Prisma P2025 record-not-found error), this update throws from inside the catch, the exception propagates out of the `for` loop and the handler, so every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped and the request fails with a 500 instead of a partial success. Wrap the bookkeeping update in its own try/catch (or use `updateMany`) so one bad reminder cannot abort the batch.

retryCount is not incremented when message or sendTo is missing

The retry bookkeeping only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. A reminder whose resolved `sendTo` is null/empty (e.g. attendee never provided `smsReminderNumber`) or whose template renders to an empty string silently falls through: nothing is scheduled, `scheduled` stays false and `retryCount` stays 0, so the cron keeps re-picking this row on every invocation until `scheduledDate` passes — exactly the unbounded-retry behaviour this PR aims to stop. These cases should also increment retryCount (or the row should be deleted).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching tests for auth/filter conditions were deleted while the caching logic remains

The entire `describe("Caching")` block (tests for `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions`) was removed, but `getAuthorizationConditions()`/`getFilterConditions()` in the service still memoize via `this.cachedAuthConditions`/`this.cachedFilterConditions` (insightsBooking.ts lines 83-95). Notably the `null` case for filter conditions is a subtle memoization branch (`undefined` vs `null`) that is now completely untested, so a regression that re-queries the DB on every call, or that caches `null` incorrectly, would go unnoticed. The tests should be ported to the new SQL expectations rather than dropped.

Loosened constructor option type lets invalid scopes compile and silently degrade to 1=0

The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (`scope: "user" | "org" | "team"`, `teamId?: number`) instead of the discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions`. Previously, passing `scope: "team"` without a `teamId` was a compile error; now it type-checks, zod validation fails in the constructor, `this.options` becomes `null`, and every query silently gets the `1=0` condition with no error or log. A caller mis-wiring the options will see an empty insights result set rather than a failure, which is very hard to diagnose. Keep the discriminated union in the constructor signature, or at minimum throw/log when `safeParse` fails.

Only the user-scope SQL is actually executed against the database; ANY() array binding is untested

The only test that runs real SQL (`$queryRaw` on `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized`) uses `scope: "user"`, whose condition contains no arrays. The org and team scope conditions rely on `"teamId" = ANY(${array})` / `"userId" = ANY(${array})` parameter binding (insightsBooking.ts lines 164, 168, 201), which is only asserted by structural `toEqual` comparison of `Prisma.Sql` objects — that cannot catch a failure of the driver to bind a JS array as a Postgres array, nor a column-type mismatch. Add integration tests that execute the org- and team-scope base conditions via `$queryRaw` and assert the returned rows.

Org-scope assertion depends on unordered query results, making the test flaky

The expectation compares the exact bound-parameter arrays `[org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]` against the SQL built from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`. Those repository calls have no `orderBy`, so PostgreSQL may return rows in any order; since `toEqual` on a `Prisma.Sql` compares the `values` array element-by-element, the test can fail non-deterministically. Either sort the ids in the service before building the condition or compare order-insensitively (e.g. assert on sorted copies of `conditions.values`).

Public findMany() removed without updating any callers

The `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method was deleted and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment instead of executing a query. No other file in the repository is touched by this PR, so any existing consumer of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` (e.g. insights tRPC routers/handlers) will fail to compile or, if dynamically typed, fail at runtime. Either keep `findMany` as a thin wrapper that runs `$queryRaw` with the base conditions, or update all call sites in the same change.

getBaseConditions can return an un-parenthesized top-level OR, breaking AND-composition by callers

`getBaseConditions()` returns the authorization SQL verbatim when there are no filters (line 75), and for `org`/`team` scope that SQL is a top-level `OR` expression such as `("teamId" = ANY($1)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true) OR (("userId" = ANY($2)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false))` with no surrounding parentheses (see the reduce at lines 171-174 and 204-207). Any consumer that interpolates the result into a larger predicate, e.g. ``WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "startTime" >= ${from}``, gets `A AND B OR (C AND D AND startTime>=...)` because `AND` binds tighter than `OR`. That silently returns bookings outside the requested date range and, worse, rows that should have been excluded by the additional predicate — an authorization-scope leak. The same applies to the public `getFilterConditions()`, which returns `("eventTypeId" = $1) OR ("eventParentId" = $1)` unwrapped when it is the only filter. All returned fragments should be wrapped in outer parentheses (e.g. `Prisma.sql`(${expr})`).

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateMany with empty data relies on implicit @updatedAt and writes on every cache refresh

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is called at the end of every `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` run (including each Google webhook delivery and cron refresh). It passes an empty `data` object and depends entirely on Prisma implicitly adding `updatedAt` to the SET clause; if that behaviour changes or the field is not `@updatedAt`, the call becomes a no-op UPDATE on every selected calendar row for the credential with no visible error. It also performs an extra write over all rows of the credential on a hot path, and per the PR description the resulting `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not consumed anywhere in the UI (the UI uses `cacheUpdatedAt` from `CalendarCache`). Either set the timestamp explicitly (`{ updatedAt: new Date() }`) or drop the call.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`sed -i ''` is macOS-only and breaks on Linux

The in-place edit uses BSD/macOS syntax `sed -i '' -E ...`. With GNU sed (Linux, CI containers) `-i ''` is parsed as an empty suffix argument followed by the empty string being treated as the script/file, so the command errors out or edits the wrong file, leaving `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` unchanged while the script still prints the success message. Use a portable approach (e.g. write to a temp file and move it, or branch on `uname`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache throws a plain Error instead of TRPCError

When the credential is not found or does not belong to the caller, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC converts unknown errors into `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500) and reports them to error logging/monitoring as server faults, instead of a 404/403. Use `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" | "FORBIDDEN", message: ... })` so the client gets a correct status and the condition is not reported as a server crash. The UI currently only shows a generic toast, so the mis-typed error also hides the real cause from the user.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp hardcoded to en-US locale and browser timezone

The timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` regardless of the user's locale (available via `useLocale()`) or the user's configured timezone/time format. Non-English users will see a US-formatted date inside an otherwise localized string, and the time is rendered in the browser timezone which may differ from the profile timezone used elsewhere in the app.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status ignores expiresAt, so expired cache rows are shown as current

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` aggregates `MAX(updatedAt)` over all `CalendarCache` rows for a credential with no `expiresAt` filter. Rows stay in the table after expiry (expiry is enforced at read time via `expiresAt: { gte: now }` in `getCachedAvailability`), so the UI will display a "Last updated" timestamp and a "Delete cached data" action for credentials whose cache is expired and no longer served. The displayed status is therefore misleading. Filter by `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` (or surface expiry explicitly).

Cache status query bypasses the calendar-cache feature gate

The handler instantiates `CalendarCacheRepository` directly rather than going through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the factory that returns `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when the calendar-cache feature is disabled. As a result, users/teams without the `calendar-cache` feature enabled will still get cache status and the "Delete cached data" action in the UI, and every `connectedCalendars` request pays an extra `groupBy` query even when the feature is off.

Migration warning comment contradicts the SQL it documents

The auto-generated warning block states the column is added "without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty", but the SQL actually adds `updatedAt` with `DEFAULT NOW()`, which is safe for non-empty tables. Leaving the stale warning in place is misleading for anyone reviewing or replaying migrations; remove or correct it.

No tests for the new cache deletion authorization or cache-status mapping

The PR adds a destructive mutation (`deleteCache`) whose only protection is an ownership check on `Credential.userId`, plus a new repository aggregation (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`) and the credential→cache mapping in `connectedCalendars.handler.ts`. None of these have unit tests: there is no test asserting that another user's credentialId is rejected, that cache rows of other credentials are not deleted, or that the `credentialId → updatedAt` map is built correctly (including credentials without cache). Given the authorization-sensitive and data-deleting nature of the handler, tests should accompany it.

UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt and googleChannelId that the function never uses

`UserWithCalendars` was widened so `allSelectedCalendars`/`userLevelSelectedCalendars` must include `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`, but nothing in this file (or in the new cache-status code, which reads `CalendarCache.updatedAt`) consumes those fields. This is an exported type used by other callers (platform libraries / API v2 / other handlers) that build the user object with only `externalId | integration | eventTypeId`; those call sites now fail to type-check and require a matching `select` change. Either revert the widening or update all construction sites.

deleteCache success does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query

The `deleteCache` mutation only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop, while the disconnect mutation explicitly invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`. In `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` the `onSuccess` prop is wired to `props.onChanged`, which is optional and undefined on the installed-apps page; the `connectedCalendars` query is also configured with `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`. Consequently, after deleting the cache the dropdown keeps showing the old "Last updated" timestamp and the delete action until a full reload. Invalidate `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in the mutation's `onSettled`/`onSuccess`.

dev:cron switched to `npx tsx` without declaring tsx as a dependency

`dev:cron` now runs `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not in `dependencies`/`devDependencies` (while the now-unused `ts-node` remains). `npx` will silently download an arbitrary latest version of `tsx` from the network on each developer machine/CI run, which is non-deterministic and fails in offline/locked-down environments. Add `tsx` as a devDependency and invoke it via the local binary.

updateManyByCredentialId typed with SelectedCalendarUpdateInput instead of the updateMany input type

`prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany` accepts `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`, but the method signature declares `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput`, which additionally permits nested relation operations (`user: { connect: ... }`, etc.). Such payloads type-check at compile time but fail at runtime when passed to `updateMany`. Narrow the parameter type to `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is now fire-and-forget; the `cancelled` flag may never be persisted

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async but are invoked inside `forEach` without `await`, and their results are no longer collected into `prismaPromises` (as the previous `remindersToDelete` array was). The handler can therefore return its HTTP response before the `workflowReminder.update({ cancelled: true })` / `delete` queries have executed. On a serverless runtime the function can be frozen/terminated right after the response, so the flag is never written and the cron job will never cancel the scheduled SendGrid email — the reminder for a cancelled booking is still delivered. The same unawaited pattern was introduced in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule) and `handleNewBooking.ts`. These calls should be awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path re-introduces the SendGrid pending-cancellation limit and leaks DB rows

When `immediateDelete` is true, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` issues the SendGrid `status: "cancel"` request straight away and returns early, without deleting or flagging the `workflowReminder` row. Two consequences: (1) every reschedule (`handleNewBooking.ts`, which passes `true`) and every workflow/step deletion still consumes one of SendGrid's max-100 pending cancellation slots — the root cause described in the PR body — so the limit can still be exhausted and subsequent cancellations silently fail; (2) for the reschedule path (where the old booking row is not deleted and therefore nothing cascades) the stale reminder row survives with `scheduled: true` and a `referenceId`, and `cancelled` left null, so it is only cleaned up when the scheduledDate finally passes. Either route the reschedule case through the deferred `cancelled` flag like cancellation, or delete the row when cancelling immediately.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation query does not restrict to EMAIL reminders with a reference id

`remindersToCancel` selects every `workflowReminder` with `cancelled: true`, without filtering on `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`, `scheduled: true` or `referenceId: { not: null }`. Today only email reminders are ever flagged, but any future/manual row with another method (or a null `referenceId`) would be POSTed to SendGrid as a `batch_id`, producing an error that — given the shared try/catch — aborts the whole cancellation loop. Add the explicit filters so this endpoint only ever handles rows it can act on.

Deferred cancellation can miss SendGrid's cancellation deadline for near-term reminders

Cancellation is deferred to a cron that runs every ~15 minutes and only picks up reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour. A booking cancelled shortly before its reminder's send time (e.g. 12 minutes before) will only have the SendGrid cancel request issued on the next cron tick, which can be less than SendGrid's required 10-minute lead time before `sendAt` — in that case the cancel is rejected/ignored and the reminder email is still sent. Worse, the `deleteMany` at line 34 removes EMAIL reminders whose `scheduledDate` is already in the past before the cancellation block runs, so such rows are dropped without any cancellation attempt and without any log. Consider cancelling immediately when `scheduledDate` is near (while keeping the deferred path for far-future reminders) so the pending-cancellation quota is still protected.

No automated coverage for the cancelled-reminder flow

This is the second attempt at fixing reminders being sent for cancelled/rescheduled bookings (the previous fix in #6991 silently stopped working in production). The PR adds a new `cancelled` field plus a new cron branch but no test asserting that cancelling or rescheduling a booking marks the reminder `cancelled: true`, that the cron issues the SendGrid cancel and removes the row, and that a failing cancellation does not block the others. Without a test the regression can recur unnoticed, as it already did.

One failing SendGrid cancellation aborts the whole cancellation loop permanently

The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop is wrapped in a single outer `try`/`catch`. If the `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` request throws for one reminder (invalid/expired batch id, already-cancelled batch, transient 4xx/5xx), the catch is hit, the loop aborts, and none of the remaining reminders in the batch are cancelled; the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected so far are never awaited either (Prisma promises are lazy), so nothing is removed from the DB. Because the next cron run re-selects the same rows ordered the same way, a single permanently-failing reminder blocks every other cancellation forever and reminder emails for cancelled/rescheduled bookings keep going out — exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. The try/catch (and the delete) should be inside the loop, per reminder.

The import block was changed from `import type { Prisma, PrismaPromise }` to a value import that still includes `Prisma`, but all `Prisma.BatchPayload` usages were removed in this diff, so `Prisma` is now unused in this file. With the repo's no-unused-vars/consistent-type-imports lint rules this fails CI; the formatting of the new import block (no trailing comma on the last specifier) will also be flagged by the prettier check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring-booking calendar deletions are pushed into apiDeletes after it is already awaited

In the recurring branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` uses an async callback inside `forEach`, so the callbacks return immediately and the `apiDeletes.push(...)` happens on later microtasks. By the time `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs at the end of the handler, `apiDeletes` is still empty, so the remote calendar events for the remaining recurring occurrences are deleted fire-and-forget (and their failures surface as unhandled rejections rather than being reported). The sibling non-credentialId branch in this same diff was correctly converted to a `for...of` loop; this branch should be too (e.g. `for (const credential of ...)` with awaited deletes pushed as promises).

The object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")`, `import("./caldavcalendar")`, … directly, which means every dynamic import is *started* the moment `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated. The resulting object holds already-pending/resolved module promises, so all ~28 app packages (and their transitive deps such as googleapis, @microsoft/..., stripe, etc.) are still pulled into the bundle and executed at startup; the only thing that changed is that the consumer now has to `await` them. To get the intended benefit the map must hold thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, and call sites must invoke them (`await appStore[key]()`). As written the PR adds async plumbing across the codebase without delivering the stated code-splitting/startup win.

Converting the `forEach` callback to `async` means `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` returns before any deletion happens, so the surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` can never observe a failure — rejections escape as unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and `return true` while the external calendar/video cancellations may not have executed. Same defect as in the vital app: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { await getCalendar(...) ... })` returns immediately, so the enclosing `try/catch` that logs errors is dead code and any failure of `calendar.deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection. The reschedule email is sent and `true` returned before the external cancellations are known to have completed, which can leave orphaned calendar/video events. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` so the awaited work is covered by the try/catch.

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` expression; it should be derived from `slotEndTime`. As written the event length is ignored, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after them passes the `end > workingHour.endTime` test. The variable is dead/duplicated code that makes the guard weaker than intended.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with `===`, condition never true

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created Dayjs objects by reference, so it is always false. The intended case (zero-length override, i.e. a date marked fully unavailable) is therefore never detected and the code falls through to the range comparisons, where a slot starting exactly at the override instant is reported as available. Use `.isSame(...)`.

false_positives.candidate:
Busy times are ignored for any slot on a day that has a date override

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, after the date-override block, `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns early and completely skips the `busy.every(...)` check below. Consequence: on any day for which the host has a date override, existing bookings and external calendar busy times are no longer taken into account, so already-booked slots are offered again and can be double booked. The early return should only mean "working-hours check is superseded by the override"; the busy-time check must still run.

Date-override day comparison is done in the server's local timezone

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` builds a Dayjs in the *server's local* timezone, while `slotStartTime` is `time.utc()` and formats in UTC. On any deployment whose process timezone is not UTC, the two date strings can differ by a day, so the override silently does not match the slot and `dateOverrideExist` stays false, falling back to normal working hours and ignoring the override entirely. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for the comparison. The same conversion also shifts overrides whose local time is near midnight onto the neighbouring UTC day, where they will never match a slot.

Multiple date overrides on the same day make all slots unavailable

`dateOverrides.find(...)` returns truthy as soon as *one* override on the slot's day does not contain the slot, and the code then returns `false` (unavailable). Users can define several override ranges for the same date (e.g. 09:00–10:00 and 14:00–15:00). With two ranges, a slot inside the first range is still rejected by the second, so no slot on that date is bookable. The check must be "unavailable only if the slot fits none of the day's overrides".

No test for the main fix (date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin)

The PR's primary claim is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events, but the only new test asserts that the existing single-user override case returns the same UTC slots for a second invitee timezone. There is no scenario with a ROUND_ROBIN event type, a fixed host with a date override and an available non-fixed host, so the new `checkIfIsAvailable` override/working-hours code path (and the regression it can cause for split availability or for days with both an override and an existing booking) is untested.

Override converted to minutes-of-day wraps across midnight and lands on the wrong day

`startTime`/`endTime` are computed as `hour()*60 + minute()` after shifting the override by `offset`. When the shift crosses midnight (e.g. an override at 22:00–23:00 organizer time viewed from a timezone 2 hours ahead becomes 00:00–01:00 of the next day), the minute-of-day values wrap: the override is then applied to the *current* invitee day at the wrong clock time, or produces `startTime > endTime` which `buildSlots` discards, dropping the availability completely. Overrides must be attributed to the invitee day they actually fall on rather than being collapsed to minutes-of-day of the day being iterated.

Working-hours check is inverted: any non-matching range marks the slot unavailable

The new check uses `workingHours.find(wh => slot is OUTSIDE wh)` and returns `false` (unavailable) if such an entry is found. A user whose schedule has more than one availability block on the same weekday (e.g. 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, the normal "lunch break" setup) will always have at least one block that does not contain the slot, so *every* slot on that day is rejected. Fixed hosts / collective events with split availability will show no slots at all. The logic must be "available if the slot fits inside at least one working-hour range for that day" (e.g. `!workingHours.some(covers)`).

`override.timeZone` is optional; undefined falls back to the server timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` relies on `TimeRange.timeZone`, which was added as optional in `packages/types/schedule.d.ts`. When a caller of `getSlots` passes date overrides without `timeZone` (every call site other than the tRPC `getSchedule` that was updated in this PR), `.tz(undefined)` silently uses the process default timezone, producing a wrong `organizerUtcOffset` and therefore slots shifted by an arbitrary amount. Either make the field required on the type used by `GetSlots` or fall back explicitly to the organizer timezone.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a constant pipeline signature, not a per-request nonce

The OAuth2 authorize request is sent with `state = pipeline.signature`, and the callback validates `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic hash of the pipeline's view classes: it is identical for every user, every org and every installation attempt (the tests hard-code `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and reuse it across different users/orgs), and it is exposed in plaintext in every authorize redirect URL. A constant, publicly known value provides no CSRF/code-injection protection, contrary to the PR description's claim that a `state` mismatch is a security check: an attacker can craft `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker code>&state=9cae...` and have the victim's pipeline exchange the attacker's code and bind the attacker's GitHub login into `github_authenticated_user`. Follow the pattern in `OAuth2LoginView`/`OAuth2CallbackView`: generate a random nonce (`secrets.token_hex()`), `pipeline.bind_state("state", nonce)`, and compare the callback value against the stored nonce.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

`GitHubInstallation.dispatch` compares the pipeline state against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with direct subscript access. `sender` is only present in an Integration's metadata when the row was written by the `installation` webhook handler; `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` only adds it when `state.get("sender")` is set (it never is in this pipeline), and the pipeline's `update_or_create` overwrites the metadata on every successful install (see `test_basic_flow`, where the stored metadata has no `sender` key). So any Integration that was last written by the pipeline, and reaches this branch (Integration row exists and is ACTIVE but has no OrganizationIntegration rows, e.g. after the org integration was removed), will raise an unhandled `KeyError` here and return a 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly whether a missing sender should fail closed.

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user validation is skipped entirely when no Integration row exists yet

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the view immediately calls `pipeline.next_step()`, so the new `github_authenticated_user` vs. installation-sender check is never performed and `build_integration` will happily claim the installation. Since GitHub installation ids are small sequential integers, an attacker can supply someone else's `installation_id` and, if no Integration row is present, bind that installation (and its repository access) to their own Sentry org — exactly the attack this PR aims to prevent. `test_github_user_mismatch` only covers the negative branch (authenticated login != `metadata["sender"]["login"]`). It performs an HTTP request to `/user` and raises `ApiError` on non-2xx responses (revoked token, GitHub 5xx, rate limiting), and may also return a non-dict payload, which would make the following `"login" not in authenticated_user_info` check raise `TypeError`. true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can skip terminating remaining processes and computes an unused variable

In `join()`, `remaining_time` is computed but never used, and when the deadline has passed the loop `break`s, so the remaining processes in `self.processes` are never waited for nor terminated (they are only daemonic, so they are killed when the parent exits, possibly mid-flush). Combined with the broken `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check on line 346, no spawn process is ever terminated at shutdown. Either drop the unused variable and terminate all processes regardless of deadline, or document why skipping is acceptable.

false_positives.candidate:
Class docstring contradicts actual process allocation and omits max_processes

The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but shards are actually bucketed round-robin into `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes, and the CLI default is a single process for all shards. The docstring also still documents a `:param topic:` that does not exist while the newly added `max_processes` parameter is undocumented.

Comma-joined shard list used as metric tag value creates unbounded cardinality

`shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` is used as the `shard` tag on `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and the per-segment `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` timing. The value is a *set* of shards that changes with every Kafka rebalance and with the `--flusher-processes` setting, so the tag value space is combinatorial rather than bounded by the number of shards, and `segment_size_bytes` is emitted per segment. This can blow up metric cardinality and makes per-shard aggregation impossible. Consider tagging with the process index or omitting the tag on high-volume metrics.

Dead method `_create_process_for_shard`

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Leaving it in is confusing because it looks like the per-shard restart path but would silently do nothing if `shard` is not in any mapping. Remove it.

No test exercises the multiprocess flusher path

Both new/updated tests pass `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher` use `threading.Thread` instead of `mp_context.Process`. The core change of this PR — spawning a real process per shard group, pickling a per-shard `SpansBuffer` into it, restarting a dead/hung process, and the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` kill/terminate paths — is therefore completely untested (and indeed broken, see the isinstance finding). Add at least one test that drives the actual spawn-process path, or a unit test of `_ensure_processes_alive` with a fake spawn process.

Shard-distribution assertion cannot detect duplicated or missing shards

`total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()); assert total_shards == 4` would also pass if the same shard were assigned to two processes while another shard was dropped entirely — exactly the kind of bug that would cause duplicate or lost segments. Assert on the union instead, e.g. that the concatenation of all lists equals `{0,1,2,3}` with no duplicates, and that the buckets are balanced.

max_processes=None/0 silently means one process per shard

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means that any caller that does not pass `max_processes` (the default, used by every direct construction such as `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py`) spawns one OS process per assigned shard, while the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1. A consumer assigned 32 partitions constructed without the option would fork 32 flusher processes, each with its own Redis connections — a large, unintended resource jump compared to the previous single-process behaviour. Additionally, because of `or`, an explicit `--flusher-processes 0` is silently reinterpreted as "one per shard" instead of being rejected. Make the default explicit (e.g. 1) and validate that the value is >= 1.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implemented behaviour and is timing-dependent

The test is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits" but asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing was committed. The implementation marks the offset complete in the worker's `finally` block even when processing raised, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the 1-second commit loop will commit them. The assertion only passes because the test breaks out of its wait loop ~0.2-0.3s after submitting, before the commit thread's first tick - it will flake as soon as timing shifts, and it does not verify the behaviour its docstring describes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Any offset that is never submitted permanently stalls commits for the partition

`get_committable_offsets()` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks as soon as an offset is not present in `all_offsets`. Offsets can be missing for reasons other than slow processing: arroyo can hand the strategy messages whose `value` is not a `BrokerValue` (the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` fails and the `except` branch then also skips recording because of the same `isinstance` check), transaction/control markers consume offsets on some topics, and anything that throws before `add_offset` leaves a hole. Once a hole exists the partition can never advance: no offsets are ever committed again, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and on restart the whole backlog is reprocessed. Track a per-partition "next expected" watermark from the messages actually received rather than requiring offset contiguity.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback. That callback mutates the StreamProcessor's staged-offset state and the underlying consumer, which the main poll thread is using concurrently; arroyo's consumer/commit path is not documented as thread-safe. This can corrupt the staged offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. committing offsets for a partition that was just revoked), and the only handling is a broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` that will then spin once per second. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. via a thread-safe queue drained in `poll()`), which is also where arroyo expects commits to happen.

Failed work items are marked complete, so failures are committed and lost

`complete_offset()` is called in the `finally` block of the worker, so a work item whose `result_processor` raised is treated exactly like a successfully processed one: its offset becomes committable and is committed, with only a log line. There is no retry, no DLQ and no metric, so a transient failure (e.g. a DB hiccup) silently drops the check result. If this at-most-once behaviour is intended it should at least emit a failure metric; otherwise the offset should not be completed on error.

Kafka integration test relies on private arroyo APIs, wall-clock sleeps and a second consumer in the same group

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest` drives the consumer with `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice), busy-loops for a fixed 5 wall-clock seconds and then asserts an exact committed offset of 5 - this depends on the background commit thread and ONCE_PER_SECOND policy firing within that window, so it will flake on a loaded CI machine. It also creates a second `confluent_kafka.Consumer` with the same `group.id` to read committed offsets, which joins the group and can trigger a rebalance/return stale offsets, and `verify_consumer.committed(partitions)` is called without a timeout so it can block indefinitely.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition reassignment

`OffsetTracker` is owned by the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets`, `outstanding` and `partition_locks` for every partition it has ever seen. On rebalance a new strategy is created but the tracker still holds the old `last_committed` values; if a partition is reassigned and the consumer must restart from an earlier offset (or the partition is assigned to another consumer and later returned), `get_committable_offsets()` will refuse to return anything `<= last_committed`, permanently stalling commits for that partition. Entries for revoked partitions are also never dropped, so the dicts grow for the lifetime of the process.

Per-message gauge emitted from every worker with identical tags

Every processed item emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` as a gauge tagged only with `identifier`. All N workers report their own queue's depth under the same metric name and tag set, so the values overwrite each other and the resulting series is meaningless, while the emission rate equals the message rate. Either tag by `worker_id`/queue index or report queue depth periodically from `poll()` instead.

Queue pool is owned by the factory but shut down by the strategy, breaking the consumer after the first rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared via `self.queue_pool`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (queue_consumer.py lines 335-342), which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. Arroyo closes the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on assignment. The second strategy therefore gets a pool whose worker threads have exited and whose queues are shut down, so every `work_queue.put(...)` raises `queue.ShutDown`. That exception is swallowed by the `except Exception` block in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, which then marks the offset as added *and* completed - so messages are silently dropped and their offsets committed. After the first rebalance the consumer stops doing any work while continuing to advance offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool must be created per strategy (or not shut down in `close()`).

Queues are unbounded and submit never applies backpressure

`queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks or rejects: if the result processor is slower than the incoming message rate, arroyo will keep reading from Kafka and the strategy will buffer the entire backlog (decoded results plus the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload` kept on `WorkItem.message`) in memory until the process OOMs. Give the queues a bounded size and raise `MessageRejected` (or block) when full, and fix the docstring.

close()/join() do not drain queues or perform a final commit

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and just calls `close()`; `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and then shuts down the pool. Because `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues, each worker exits after finishing at most one more item, so all still-queued work items are discarded. Additionally no commit is attempted after the workers stop, so offsets for items that completed since the last 1-second commit tick are never committed. Arroyo's contract for `join(timeout)` is to flush outstanding work and commit before returning; as written every shutdown/rebalance drops in-flight work and re-reads a window of messages (duplicate processing) on restart.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every non-granting cached check now triggers a full DB permission re-query

`getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` no longer short-circuit on the permission cache (the cache lookups were removed), and `Check` only returns early when the cached permissions grant access. Consequently every Check for a resource the user is not (yet) known to have access to performs the full store path again (basic role, teams, `GetUserPermissions`) instead of being served from the 30s cache. The denial cache only bounds this per (action, name, folder) tuple, so workloads that check many distinct objects (e.g. per-item authorization over a large dashboard set) will issue one permission query per object per TTL, a large increase in DB load compared to the previous behaviour. Consider limiting the DB fallback (e.g. only when the cached entry is older than a short grace period, or once per user/action per interval).

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually exercise the short-circuit and its comment is wrong

In "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permission cache is seeded with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. not allowed. Additionally `s.store`/`s.permissionStore` are the default empty `fakeStore`, which returns no permissions. The assertion `resp.Allowed == false` therefore holds even if the denial cache were ignored entirely, so the test gives no coverage of the new early-return path. Seed the permission cache with `true` (and/or a store that grants access) so the test fails if the denial cache is not consulted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key can collide across different resources (underscore delimiter)

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user UID, action, resource name and parent folder with `_` as the only separator. Resource names and folder UIDs in Grafana may legally contain underscores, so distinct checks produce identical keys, e.g. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") both yield `...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. Because `Check` now returns an immediate deny on a key hit (service.go:117), a legitimate deny for one resource will spuriously deny access to a different resource for the whole 30s TTL, with no way for the caller to recover. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or hash/length-prefix the components.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache has unbounded key cardinality (one entry per user/action/name/folder)

The denial cache key includes the requested resource name and parent folder, so the number of entries grows with the number of distinct objects ever denied, per user and action. With a local in-memory cache that has no size limit (see `cache.NewLocalCache` in pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:88), a user or service scanning many resources they cannot access (thousands of dashboards) will populate thousands of entries within each 30s window, which can translate into significant memory pressure on large instances. A bounded/LRU cache or a coarser key is needed.

Denial is cached even when the deny came from a stale folder tree, stacking staleness

When the cached permissions do not grant access, the code re-queries permissions from the DB, but `checkInheritedPermissions`/`buildFolderTree` still use the 30s-cached folder tree (service.go:609-635). If the folder tree is stale and does not yet contain a freshly created parent folder, the check denies and that deny is then stored in `permDenialCache` for another full TTL. The staleness windows add up (up to ~2x shortCacheTTL), so a user who just created a nested folder/dashboard can keep being denied even after the permission refresh - exactly the scenario this PR aims to fix. Either bypass/refresh the folder tree on the fallback path, or do not cache denials that were produced by an inherited-permission lookup against a cached tree.

Denial key uses raw subject UID while permission key uses resolved UID

The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw subject identifier from the request), whereas `userPermCacheKey` is built from `userIdentifiers.UID` resolved via `GetUserIdentifiers` (which treats numeric subjects as internal IDs). For a subject passed as `user:<numeric id>` the two caches are keyed on different identifiers, so the same user gets duplicate/independent denial entries depending on the subject form used by the caller, and denial entries cannot be reasoned about together with the permission entries. Resolve identifiers first and key both caches on the same resolved UID.

permissionCacheUsage metric is now misleading

`permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with "true" on a denial-cache hit (line 118), mixing two different caches into one hit-rate metric, and it is incremented with "false" at line 137 even when the permission cache was actually hit but simply did not grant access. The resulting cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts for the permission cache will report wrong values. Use a separate label/metric for the denial cache and only report "false" on a real permission-cache miss.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing `key` prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in the filtered rule list

In the `rules.map(...)` loop the `grafana` branch renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` without a `key`, while the other two branches still pass `key={key}`. The previously rendered `GrafanaRuleLoader` had `key={key}`. React will emit "Each child in a list should have a unique key" warnings and, because this list grows incrementally via infinite scrolling, element reuse becomes index-based, which can cause incorrect DOM/state reuse (e.g. open menus or skeletons attached to the wrong rule) when batches are appended.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is shown but the silence drawer can never open without a ruler rule

`SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, and `rule` (the ruler rule) is `undefined` when this component is used from the new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only `promRule`). Meanwhile AlertRuleMenu now enables the "Silence notifications" item based on the Grafana Prometheus abilities, so the item is visible but clicking it only toggles `showSilenceDrawer` and nothing is rendered — a dead menu entry for every Grafana rule in the list view.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated rule group detection dropped from useAllRulerRuleAbilities

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to mark Update/Delete/Duplicate/Pause as unsupported for federated (Mimir cross-tenant) rule groups. After merging into `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, `isFederated` is hardcoded to `false` with only a TODO. Users will now be offered Edit/Delete/Duplicate on federated Mimir rules, which cannot be edited through this UI and will fail server-side. If the group information is not available in `RuleGroupIdentifierV2`, this needs another source rather than a silent `false`.

Grafana-managed recording rules lose Pause and Export support in the new ability hook

`useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` uses `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` where the ruler-based equivalent used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` (true for both alerting and recording Grafana rules). As a result `Pause`, `Restore`, `DeletePermanently` and `ModifyExport` are reported as unsupported for Grafana-managed *recording* rules, even though these rules can be paused and exported. In the list view (which now relies solely on these abilities) pausing/exporting a Grafana recording rule becomes impossible.

New `provenance` field on GrafanaPromRuleDTO is untested and unverified against the API

`provenance?: string` is added to `GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase` and is now the only signal used by `isProvisionedPromRule` / `GrafanaRuleListItem`'s `isProvisioned` and by the ability hooks to block editing of provisioned rules in the list view. No test (including the new `rulerRuleToPromRule` helper in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx) sets this field, so if the Grafana Prometheus rules endpoint does not return `provenance`, provisioned rules will be rendered as editable/deletable in the list view and nothing will catch it.

Pause and Delete menu items are still gated on `rulerRule`, so they disappear in the new list view

The menu now computes Grafana-Prometheus-based abilities (`grafanaPauseAbility`, `grafanaDeleteAbility`) so actions can work without ruler data, but the render conditions were not updated: line 123 requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` for the pause item and line 165 requires `rulerRule` for the delete item. The new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem -> RuleActionsButtons) only passes `promRule`, never `rulerRule`, so Pause/Resume and Delete silently vanish from the rule menu in the alert list for all Grafana-managed rules. The newly added ability checks have no effect for these two actions.

Stale comment and variable name after removing the ruler prefetch

The ruler `getGrafanaRulerGroup` prefetch was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX ... doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded" and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behaviour that no longer exists and will mislead readers about what this block does.

Test asserts exactly 4 menu items, codifying the loss of Delete/Pause actions

The test grants `AlertingRuleDelete` and `AlertingRuleUpdate` both globally and on the folder, yet asserts `menuItems.length === 4` and never uses the newly declared `ui.menuItems.delete` selector. Because the menu still requires a ruler rule for Delete and Pause (AlertRuleMenu lines 123/165), those items are absent — and this assertion now locks that regression in, so a future fix restoring Delete/Pause would break the test instead of the test catching the missing actions. The test should explicitly assert the expected presence of Delete and Pause for a user with those permissions.

`logWarning` called from the render phase

`getEditableIdentifier` is invoked during render and calls `logWarning(...)` as a side effect when no identifier can be derived. Render-phase side effects run on every re-render (and twice per render under React StrictMode), so a single rule whose identifier cannot be constructed will repeatedly emit the same analytics warning. This should be moved into an effect or deduplicated.

`returnTo` query param dropped from the rule view link

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader` built the href as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops the `returnTo` parameter, so navigating from the rule list into a rule detail page loses the "return to previous" affordance that the rest of the alerting UI relies on.

skipToken path returns `Duplicate` as supported and allowed, leaking the action onto non-Grafana rules

`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(skipToken, ...)` calls `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)`. With `rule === undefined`, `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` returns `loading: false`, so `MaybeSupported = AlwaysSupported` and `duplicateSupported = true`; `Duplicate` therefore evaluates to `[true, ctx.hasPermission(grafana rules create)]`. Because AlertRuleMenu ORs the ruler and Grafana abilities, a user holding Grafana `AlertingRuleCreate` will see the "Duplicate" action on data-source (Mimir/Loki/Prometheus) rules even when the ruler-based ability says it is unsupported/not allowed, and the clone flow will then fail. The skip path should produce all-false abilities. Note the unit tests mock these hooks, so this is not caught by RulesTable.test.tsx.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
New interpolation test mocks replace() in a way that contradicts real `$__auto` handling

The test's `replace` mock substitutes `$__auto` with `5m`, and the test then asserts the executed expr is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. Loki's real `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately removes `__auto`, `__interval`, `__range` (and their variants) from `scopedVars` so that they are interpolated on the backend with the *split* time range; a real `templateSrv.replace` would leave `$__auto` untouched here. The test therefore asserts behaviour that does not occur in production and would not catch a regression where `$__auto` is prematurely resolved against the full range.
