false_positives.candidate:
Error and replay-event timestamps are compared in different units

`gen_request_data` interleaves error messages with replay breadcrumbs by comparing `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"]` against `event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from the nodestore event payload and is epoch **seconds** (~1.7e9), while rrweb replay events carry epoch **milliseconds** (~1.75e12). Every error therefore compares as smaller than every replay event, so in production all errors will be flushed to the front of the log list instead of being placed chronologically, which is the whole point of the merge. The new unit test (`test_get_request_data`) uses second-scale timestamps for the replay events too, so it cannot catch this; a test with realistic millisecond rrweb timestamps is needed.

`Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always true, so the guard is dead

`normalizeDateTimeParams(selection.datetime)` always returns an object (possibly empty), so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` can never be false and the `enabled` condition reduces to the feature check alone. If the intent was to avoid firing the request before page filters are ready (e.g. checking for a statsPeriod/start+end), the condition needs to inspect the actual fields; as written it provides no protection and will issue a request with no date range.

60s processing deadline may be too short for a 100-identity batch and breaks the task chain

`check_auth_identities` iterates up to `chunk_size` (default 100) identities and calls `provider.refresh_identity()` for each, which performs an external HTTP round trip per identity. With `processing_deadline_duration=60` the worker will kill the task once the deadline passes; because `check_auth.apply_async(...)` is only executed at the very end of the function, a deadline kill also drops the self-rescheduling call, halting the chained scan of remaining identities until the next scheduled run. Either reduce the chunk size or set a deadline that bounds 100 sequential network calls.

get_environment_info issues an extra event lookup per issue and swallows errors as 'no-environment'

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (a Snuba/eventstore lookup) plus `get_environment()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment, i.e. up to 5 extra queries per comment on top of the existing top-issues query. In addition, the blanket `except Exception` logs `get_environment_info.no-environment` with `extra={"error": e}`, which both mislabels real failures (timeouts, Snuba errors) as 'no environment' and loses the traceback (no `exc_info`/`logger.exception`), making such failures effectively invisible.

Serializer accepts reports with neither `timestamp` nor `age`

`age` and `timestamp` are both declared `required=False` and the `validate_age`/`validate_timestamp` hooks only reject the case where *both* are present. A report containing neither field passes validation even though both the Working Draft and Editor's Draft require one of them, so malformed payloads are silently accepted and counted. A `validate()` method asserting exactly one of the two is present would close the gap (and there is no test covering this case).

TabularColumn.name is typed as the field-key generic instead of string

`TabularColumn<TFields>` declares `name: TFields`, the same type as `key`. `name` is a human-readable display label (the new table explicitly supports custom names such as 'Count of Span Duration'), so once a caller instantiates `TabularColumn<'http.request_method' | 'count(span.duration)'>` the display name becomes impossible to set without a cast. `name` should be `string`.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs, not group IDs

Both explain the exact same consequences regarding fallback to 'all-groups' and broken `UserModel.GROUPS`/`getUsersCount` filtering.

false_positives.candidate:
NullPointerException when the "Groups" resource-type resource does not exist

In `hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes)`, when no resource is found for the group the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and then immediately dereferences the result (`policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and `resource.getScopes()`), without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource` returns `null` whenever `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false (e.g. the realm has an admin-permissions client but `adminPermissionsEnabled` is false) or when the resource named `Groups` simply does not exist. The latter is reachable in practice: `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` returns early if the admin permissions client already exists, so realms that enabled FGAP v2 before the `Groups` resource type was added never get the `Groups` resource or the new `manage-membership`/`manage-members`/`view-members` scopes. Any group permission check in such a realm then fails with a NPE (HTTP 500) instead of a clean deny. Add a null guard (and consider a migration/upgrade path for already-initialized admin permission clients).

Scope loop does not verify that the granted permission belongs to the evaluated resource

The result loop in `GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission` accepts any returned `Permission` whose scope list intersects the expected scopes, without checking `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())`. The analogous `UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission` (same file layout, line ~123) explicitly performs that check, which indicates the evaluation result can contain permissions for resources other than the one being evaluated (e.g. resource-type level resources). Without the check, access to one group resource can be granted by a permission evaluated for a different resource. Please align the two implementations.

V1 group permission management breaks when both FGAP v1 and v2 features are enabled

`MgmtPermissionsV2` now overrides `groups()` to return `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `isPermissionsEnabled`, `setPermissionsEnabled`, `resource`, `getPermissions` and `*Permission` methods all throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm)` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` as soon as `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled, independently of `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ`. Therefore, with both preview features enabled:

- `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (registered because v1 is enabled) handles `GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent` by calling `management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)` → `UnsupportedOperationException`, so deleting any group fails with an internal server error.
- `GroupResource.getManagementPermissions()` / `setManagementPermissionsEnabled()` (guarded only by the v1 feature flag) call `permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(...)` / `setPermissionsEnabled(...)` → HTTP 500 instead of the previous behaviour.

Before this change `MgmtPermissionsV2` inherited the working V1 `GroupPermissions` for these management operations. Either keep returning the V1 management implementation for these paths or make the listener/endpoints v2-aware.

getResourceName has no branch for the new Groups resource type

`getResourceName` resolves human-readable names only for the `Users` resource type (`All users` or the username) and otherwise falls back to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Group resources are created in `getOrCreateResource` with only a name (the group ID) and no display name, so permissions scoped to a single group will be reported with a `null` name in the policy/permission representation shown in the admin console. A `Groups` branch is needed that returns `All groups` for the resource-type resource and the group name/path for an individual group (and that handles a stale resource whose group no longer exists).

switch on resourceType throws NullPointerException for a null resource type

`getOrCreateResource` now does `switch (resourceType) { case CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE -> ... default -> throw new IllegalStateException(...) }`. A Java `switch` over a `String` throws `NullPointerException` when the selector is null, so callers that pass a null resource type now get an unhandled NPE (HTTP 500) instead of the previous `IllegalStateException("Could not map resource object ...")`/validation error. Add an explicit null check before the switch so the failure surfaces as a validation error.

Javadoc of requireManageMembers and getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is wrong

The Javadoc added for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` says it throws `ForbiddenException` if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false, but the implementation checks `canManageMembers(GroupModel)` — the copy/pasted reference documents the wrong contract. Likewise, the Javadoc of `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` (line 145) says "@return Stream of IDs of groups" while the method returns a `Set<String>`. Both should be corrected since this interface is the contract documentation for the new FGAP evaluators.

Removal of the global view short-circuit causes a policy evaluation per group

`getGroups` previously computed `boolean canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView()` once and only fell back to the per-group check when the global check failed; the same pattern was removed from `GroupResource.getSubGroups`. Now `canView(g)` is invoked for every group in the result. With FGAP v2 that means, for an admin without the `view-users`/`manage-users` roles, one `resourceStore.findByName` lookup plus a full authorization policy evaluation per returned group even when a single "all groups" view permission already grants access. For realms with large group lists this multiplies the cost of the group listing endpoints; consider restoring a cheap global short-circuit.

false_positives.candidate:
Java ChoiceFormat / single-brace placeholders break i18next message in account UI

`error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. This file is consumed by the React/i18next based account console, where interpolation uses the double-brace syntax (see `backTo=Back to {{app}}` on line 3 and `error-invalid-length='{{0}}' must have a length between {{1}} and {{2}}.` on line 140). Single-brace placeholders are not interpolated by i18next, and `{2,choice,...}` is Java MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat syntax that i18next cannot evaluate, so the user will see the literal text `{0}`, `{1}` and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` instead of the actual limits and pluralized word.

Java ChoiceFormat syntax introduced into admin UI i18next bundle

`error-invalid-multivalued-size` now uses `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` plus a Java ChoiceFormat expression `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`. The admin console translates these keys with i18next (double-brace interpolation, as used by the other `{{0}}`-style error keys in this bundle), which neither substitutes single-brace placeholders nor understands ChoiceFormat. The message will be rendered verbatim to administrators, including the raw choice expression.

Malformed character class makes English-file path derivation match too much

`replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` contains the class `[a-zA-Z-_]`, where the trailing `-_` is parsed by java.util.regex as the range 0x2D..0x5F. That range covers `-`, `.`, `/`, digits, `:` and all upper-case letters, so the pattern can match far beyond the file name: for an absolute path that contains an underscore in any parent directory (e.g. a CI workspace like `/build_dir/keycloak/themes/.../messages_de.properties`) the greedy match starts at that earlier underscore and the whole path segment chain is replaced, producing a bogus English path and an immediate build failure. Escape the dash (`[a-zA-Z_-]`) and/or derive the sibling file from `File#getName()` only.

Missing English counterpart aborts the build with an opaque RuntimeException

If the derived `_en.properties` file does not exist (community-only bundles, base `messages.properties` files whose name does not match the locale regex, or any path-derivation mistake), `verifySafeHtml` throws a raw `RuntimeException`. `verify()` only catches `IOException`, so this escapes the Mojo as an unhandled runtime exception instead of a `MojoExecutionException` or a collected verification message, giving maintainers a stack trace rather than an actionable error.

Diff substring can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException while reporting a violation

The common-prefix (`start`) and common-suffix (`end`) counters are computed independently and can overlap when the sanitized string differs in length from the input (the sanitizer regularly adds characters, e.g. missing close tags). For example value="aba" and sanitized="abba" yields start=2 and end=2, so `value.substring(2, 3-2)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The verifier then crashes with an index error instead of reporting the illegal HTML it just detected. Clamp the indices so that `start + end <= min(value.length(), sanitized.length())`.

Anchor-mismatch message does not identify the file or key

The message `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string"` omits both the properties file and the message key, unlike the HTML violation message a few lines above which includes `key` and `file`. Since the plugin runs over hundreds of bundles, a contributor seeing only this line cannot tell which translation needs fixing.

No test asserts that valid translations produce no findings

All four tests only assert that a violation message is present. There is no test feeding a legitimate translation (e.g. a `_de` file containing the same `<b>`/`<a href="...">` markup as its `_en` counterpart, or a message with a `{n,choice,...}` pattern) and asserting the result list is empty. Without such a case, false positives introduced by the normalization logic (unescaping, `<!-- -->` stripping, choice-format whitelist) would go unnoticed and break the whole build.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract method getShortcut() on public SPI interface breaks existing grant-type providers

`getShortcut()` is added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` without a `default` implementation. Any third-party/custom OAuth2 grant type provider compiled against a previous version will no longer compile, and an already-deployed jar will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates all grant factories and calls `getShortcut()`, which happens during server startup. Consider providing a `default` implementation (e.g. derived from the id, or returning null handled gracefully) to keep the SPI backwards compatible.

postInit() can fail with NPE and silently accepts colliding shortcuts registered later

In `postInit()` the shortcut returned by a grant factory is put directly into a `ConcurrentHashMap`. A custom (or future) factory returning `null` from `getShortcut()` makes `grantsByShortcuts.put(null, grantName)` throw a `NullPointerException`, aborting server startup with an obscure error instead of a meaningful validation message. In addition, the duplicate-shortcut validation (size comparison) runs only in `postInit()`; the lazy refresh paths `getShortcutByGrantType()`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut()` (lines 106-137) overwrite existing entries without any duplicate check, so a dynamically deployed grant reusing an existing shortcut would silently corrupt the mapping and make token IDs decode to the wrong grant type. The two maps are also updated with two independent `put` calls, so a concurrent reader can observe one map updated and the other not.

Access tokens issued for offline_access are encoded with session type "on" (online)

`createTokenResponse()` creates the access token (and thus the encoded session type) before `responseBuilder.generateRefreshToken()` converts/creates the offline session, and before the online user session is removed a few lines below (`session.sessions().removeUserSession(realm, userSession)` when the refresh token is of type offline). At the time `initToken()` runs, `userSession.isOffline()` is still false, so an access token obtained together with an offline refresh token gets the `on` (online) session-type prefix even though no online session exists afterwards. The same ordering exists in `ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType`. Since the stated purpose of the encoding is to let endpoints look up only the session type recorded in the token, this will lead to failed/incorrect session lookups for offline tokens once consumers rely on the value.

Removal of Context copy constructor and new hard dependency on non-null formParams

The public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` is removed from this server-spi-private class; any subclass or extension code that used it (e.g. to wrap/derive a grant context) will no longer compile. At the same time the remaining constructor now dereferences `formParams` (`formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`), so callers that previously could pass `null` form params now get a `NullPointerException`. If the copy constructor must go, the change should be noted as a breaking SPI change, and the constructor should tolerate a null `formParams`.

value_from_cursor returns raw int for a datetime column

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor()` returns `cursor.value` unchanged (integer/float), but `BasePaginator.build_queryset()` injects it into a raw SQL `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` clause. Since the endpoint orders by `-datetime`, the value must be converted back to a `datetime` as `DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor()` does. As written, following any cursor will either raise a database type error or silently compare a timestamp column against an integer, returning wrong pages. Additionally, cursor values produced by `DateTimePaginator` (milliseconds) and this paginator are not interchangeable, so a client toggling `optimized_pagination` between requests will feed incompatible cursors to the other paginator.

Silently clamping negative offsets masks invalid cursors and is inconsistent for prev cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes `BasePaginator.get_result()` for every paginator in the codebase: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced an error, now silently returns the first page as if the cursor were `offset=0`, while the cursors returned in the response are built from the original negative `cursor.offset` (see `_build_next_values`/`_build_prev_values`), producing inconsistent/incorrect next/prev links. For `is_prev` cursors the negative offset is still passed through and will raise Django's `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` (a 500) rather than a `BadPaginationError`. Negative offsets should be validated and rejected explicitly in one place.

Extra-row trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice offset

The check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` compares the number of fetched rows against the un-clamped `offset`, but the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which can differ from `offset` after clamping or in the negative-offset branch). When they differ, the extra look-ahead row is not dropped, so a previous-page response can contain `limit + 1` items / an item that belongs to the adjacent page. Use `start_offset` consistently (same issue exists in the `BasePaginator` copy at line 192).

"admin-only" gate is actually satisfied by any member of an open-membership org

The comment says the optimized path is enabled only for "authorized administrators", but the condition uses `member.has_global_access`, which is true for every member of an organization with open membership (and for any member whose role grants global access), not just admins/owners. Combined with the new unvalidated negative-offset path in `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, this lets ordinary members reach code that bypasses the normal offset bounds and crashes the request. If this is meant to be admin-only, check the actual role/permission (e.g. superuser or `org:admin`); the claim that "permissions are checked at the queryset level" in paginator.py is also unsupported for this path.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including the negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` endpoint branch are added with no unit or API tests. Given that the class as written raises `TypeError` on datetime keys and `ValueError` on negative slices, even a single test exercising the new query parameter would have caught the breakage. Tests should cover: optimized path with/without a cursor, negative offsets, and unauthorized callers falling back to `DateTimePaginator`.

Misleading comment documents negative offsets as a supported feature

The added comment states that `Cursor` now "allows negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no behavior changed here (offsets were never validated) and downstream consumers cannot handle negative offsets: Django querysets reject negative slice bounds and `OffsetPaginator`/`ChainPaginator` explicitly raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Documenting an unsupported, user-controllable value as a feature invites more code to rely on it; either add real validation here or drop the comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows two concurrent builds of the same key

`BuildIndex` no longer holds `cacheMu` for the duration of the build; it only locks when inserting into the cache. Because `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` checks `GetIndex` and then calls `BuildIndex` without any per-key serialization, two callers (e.g. a search request and a watch event for the same namespace/group/resource) can now build the same index concurrently. For file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New` on the same directory `b.opts.Root/<ns>/<resource>.<group>` at the same time, which can fail or corrupt the on-disk index; both also increment `IndexMetrics.IndexTenants` and the second cache write silently discards the first index (leaking its open bleve index/file handles). Some form of per-key locking (e.g. a keyed mutex / single-flight) is needed to keep the previous mutual exclusion while still allowing different keys to build in parallel.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same race condition in BuildIndex caused by moving the cacheMu lock from covering the whole function to only covering the final cache insertion, allowing multiple goroutines to concurrently build the index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu, racing with BuildIndex writes

`TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `b.cacheMu` (read) lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes into `b.cache` under a short-lived write lock (lines 137-139). This is a genuine data race that Go turns into a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map iteration and map write"), which crashes the process. The new call site makes it reachable: `searchSupport.init` starts the watch-event goroutine (search.go lines 207-213) and only afterwards logs `s.search.TotalDocs()` (search.go line 216); any watch event handled in that goroutine can call `getOrCreateIndex` -> `build` -> `BuildIndex`, writing the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency bug: `TotalDocs()` iterates over `b.cache` without synchronization/locking, which races with concurrent map writes in `BuildIndex` triggered by the newly started event watcher goroutine.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancel function leaked when Init fails in NewResourceServer

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but on the new error path `s.Init(ctx)` -> `return nil, err` (lines 258-262) `cancel()` is never called. The context is never cancelled, so any background work tied to it (and the context itself) is leaked, and the partially-initialized server's goroutines (e.g. the SQL poller / watch goroutines started during `search.init`) keep running for the lifetime of the process even though the constructor reported failure. `go vet`'s lostcancel check will also flag this. Call `cancel()` before returning the error.

Full index build now happens synchronously inside the constructor with no deadline or cancellation

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` with the server's own background context, which runs `lifecycle.Init`, the complete search index build over every namespace, and `initWatcher`. The constructor is invoked from the service-wiring path, so Grafana/storage-server startup is blocked for as long as indexing takes (minutes for large installations) and there is no way for the caller to pass a deadline or cancel the work - the caller's context is ignored and the internal context is only cancelled by `Stop`, which can't run yet. Consider accepting a context (or running the index build in the background and gating only search on it) so startup cannot hang indefinitely.

After Stop(), requests are no longer rejected because no method checks initErr anymore

`Stop` communicates shutdown exclusively by setting `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", which used to be surfaced because every RPC method began with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil`. Those checks were all removed in this PR, so `s.initErr` is now write-only dead state: after `Stop` cancels the background context, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/blob calls still execute and will fail with opaque "context canceled" errors or operate against a torn-down backend instead of returning the clear "service is stopping" error. A explicit stopped/closed flag checked by the public methods (or returning an error from the entry points) is needed to preserve the previous contract.

Shared err and totalBatchesIndexed are mutated from errgroup goroutines (data race)

Inside `init`, each `group.Go` closure assigns to the enclosing `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments the enclosing `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these run concurrently, so both are unsynchronized writes to shared variables: `go test -race` will flag it, the reported batch count can be wrong, and the `err` returned by one goroutine can be overwritten by another before `group.Wait()` observes it, so a build failure may be silently hidden or a spurious error attributed. Use local variables inside the closure (`idxErr := ...; return idxErr`) and an atomic counter.

BuildIndex span context is still discarded, so child spans do not nest under it

This PR's stated goal is fixing trace propagation (the callers in search.go and sql/backend.go were changed from `_, span :=` to `ctx, span :=`), but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and the builder callback keeps using the caller's context. As a result the storage `ListIterator` spans emitted while building are siblings of the `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex` span rather than children, leaving BuildIndex as a leaf in traces and defeating the purpose of the change.

The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` target (and therefore exercises the new eager `NewResourceServer` initialization path) is now skipped for postgres with only a TODO comment. Combined with the existing sqlite skip, this leaves mysql as the sole DB covered, so a startup regression specific to postgres - plausible given init now runs synchronously at construction - would go undetected. The skip should reference a tracking issue or the failure should be diagnosed before merge.

false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is owned by the factory but shut down by the strategy, breaking the consumer after the first rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared via `self.queue_pool`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (queue_consumer.py lines 335-342), which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. Arroyo closes the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on assignment. The second strategy therefore gets a pool whose worker threads have exited and whose queues are shut down, so every `work_queue.put(...)` raises `queue.ShutDown`. That exception is swallowed by the `except Exception` block in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, which then marks the offset as added *and* completed - so messages are silently dropped and their offsets committed. After the first rebalance the consumer stops doing any work while continuing to advance offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool must be created per strategy (or not shut down in `close()`).

Queues are unbounded and submit never applies backpressure

`queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks or rejects: if the result processor is slower than the incoming message rate, arroyo will keep reading from Kafka and the strategy will buffer the entire backlog (decoded results plus the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload` kept on `WorkItem.message`) in memory until the process OOMs. Give the queues a bounded size and raise `MessageRejected` (or block) when full, and fix the docstring.

close()/join() do not drain queues or perform a final commit

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and just calls `close()`; `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and then shuts down the pool. Because `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues, each worker exits after finishing at most one more item, so all still-queued work items are discarded. Additionally no commit is attempted after the workers stop, so offsets for items that completed since the last 1-second commit tick are never committed. Arroyo's contract for `join(timeout)` is to flush outstanding work and commit before returning; as written every shutdown/rebalance drops in-flight work and re-reads a window of messages (duplicate processing) on restart.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback. That callback mutates the StreamProcessor's staged-offset state and the underlying consumer, which the main poll thread is using concurrently; arroyo's consumer/commit path is not documented as thread-safe. This can corrupt the staged offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. committing offsets for a partition that was just revoked), and the only handling is a broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` that will then spin once per second. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. via a thread-safe queue drained in `poll()`), which is also where arroyo expects commits to happen.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition reassignment

`OffsetTracker` is owned by the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets`, `outstanding` and `partition_locks` for every partition it has ever seen. On rebalance a new strategy is created but the tracker still holds the old `last_committed` values; if a partition is reassigned and the consumer must restart from an earlier offset (or the partition is assigned to another consumer and later returned), `get_committable_offsets()` will refuse to return anything `<= last_committed`, permanently stalling commits for that partition. Entries for revoked partitions are also never dropped, so the dicts grow for the lifetime of the process.

Any offset that is never submitted permanently stalls commits for the partition

`get_committable_offsets()` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks as soon as an offset is not present in `all_offsets`. Offsets can be missing for reasons other than slow processing: arroyo can hand the strategy messages whose `value` is not a `BrokerValue` (the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` fails and the `except` branch then also skips recording because of the same `isinstance` check), transaction/control markers consume offsets on some topics, and anything that throws before `add_offset` leaves a hole. Once a hole exists the partition can never advance: no offsets are ever committed again, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and on restart the whole backlog is reprocessed. Track a per-partition "next expected" watermark from the messages actually received rather than requiring offset contiguity.

Failed work items are marked complete, so failures are committed and lost

`complete_offset()` is called in the `finally` block of the worker, so a work item whose `result_processor` raised is treated exactly like a successfully processed one: its offset becomes committable and is committed, with only a log line. There is no retry, no DLQ and no metric, so a transient failure (e.g. a DB hiccup) silently drops the check result. If this at-most-once behaviour is intended it should at least emit a failure metric; otherwise the offset should not be completed on error.

Kafka integration test relies on private arroyo APIs, wall-clock sleeps and a second consumer in the same group

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest` drives the consumer with `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice), busy-loops for a fixed 5 wall-clock seconds and then asserts an exact committed offset of 5 - this depends on the background commit thread and ONCE_PER_SECOND policy firing within that window, so it will flake on a loaded CI machine. It also creates a second `confluent_kafka.Consumer` with the same `group.id` to read committed offsets, which joins the group and can trigger a rebalance/return stale offsets, and `verify_consumer.committed(partitions)` is called without a timeout so it can block indefinitely.

Per-message gauge emitted from every worker with identical tags

Every processed item emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` as a gauge tagged only with `identifier`. All N workers report their own queue's depth under the same metric name and tag set, so the values overwrite each other and the resulting series is meaningless, while the emission rate equals the message rate. Either tag by `worker_id`/queue index or report queue depth periodically from `poll()` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is numeric-keyed but is used with the `datetime` column

Date-keyed querysets require `DateTimePaginator`-style key handling (the `multiplier` conversion).

true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator now silently clamps negative cursor offsets, producing inconsistent cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the behavior of every paginator derived from `BasePaginator` (issues, audit logs, many list endpoints). Previously a negative offset in a client-supplied cursor surfaced as an error from the ORM; now the query silently starts at row 0 while `build_cursor` is still handed the original negative `cursor.offset`. `_build_next_values` then computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the negative value and `_build_prev_values` treats the negative offset as "has_prev", so the returned next/prev cursors point at positions that do not correspond to the rows actually returned, causing skipped or duplicated rows on subsequent pages. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly rather than clamped.

Prev-page trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice start

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the extra-row trim condition `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` uses the raw `cursor.offset`, while the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which may differ, e.g. clamped to 0 or negative). When `offset` is negative the comparison can never be true (or is true for the wrong row count), so the extra look-behind row fetched for `is_prev` cursors is not dropped and leaks into the returned page, duplicating a row the client already saw. The condition should compare against `start_offset + limit + extra`.

Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced 10x reduction in the maximum redirect-chain depth: traces whose parent/child redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to the correct `set_key`, so their spans get split across multiple segments and are emitted as separate (incorrect) segments. If the reduction is intentional it should be stated in the PR and the caveat comment kept; otherwise the original bound should be restored.

Eviction silently drops spans with a hardcoded limit and no metric/log

`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` trims segments to a hardcoded 1000 spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured value and is no longer used anywhere, so the setting has no effect and the two numbers disagree; (2) the previous code path in `_load_segment_data` that dropped oversized segments emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and `logger.error`, and that observability was removed in this PR. Now span data is discarded with no metric, log, or configuration, making truncated segments undetectable in production.

zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting span timestamps/scores

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. The scores are `end_timestamp_precise` values used to order spans for eviction. If the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a redelivered/duplicated span that landed under a different key before the redirect was established), its score becomes the sum of two ~1.7e9 timestamps, making it the newest member forever and causing `zpopmin` to evict legitimate newer spans instead. The merges should specify `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) to preserve timestamp semantics.

`max_segment_spans` is now dead configuration

The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere; the effective limit is the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua`. Callers that set this parameter will silently get no behavior change. Either wire the value through to the Lua script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

Module docstring still describes Redis sets after the switch to sorted sets

The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`) scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted at insert time when a segment exceeds the limit. The docstring (step 3 "Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`" and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes plain sets and says nothing about scoring or eviction, so readers will have the wrong mental model of the key types and of the fact that spans can be dropped.

No test for the new insert-time eviction behavior

The headline change of this PR is eviction during insert (`zpopmin` once a segment exceeds 1000 spans) plus the set→sorted-set migration, but no test exercises a segment larger than the limit. Existing tests only cover 4-5 span segments, so neither the trimming threshold, the choice of which spans are discarded (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`), nor the removal of the old `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data` is verified. A regression in the Lua arithmetic (e.g. off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`, or the `span_count == 0` fallback) would go unnoticed.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new public paginator with non-trivial branching (negative-offset path, prev-cursor extra-row trimming, `enable_advanced_features` flag) and it is already wired into a production endpoint, yet no tests are added for it or for the audit-log endpoint's new `optimized_pagination` code path. The datetime/negative-slice failures in this class would have been caught by a single test.

Misleading comment claims a behavior change that was not made

The added comment says "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no code changed here — `Cursor` always accepted negative offsets, and callers (e.g. `OffsetPaginator`) are the ones that validate them. The comment implies `Cursor` now intentionally supports negative offsets as a feature, which will mislead future readers into assuming downstream paginators handle them safely (they do not; Django rejects negative slice starts).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Using an opaque 64-bit hash instead of the sorted ids themselves means two different project sets in the same organization can map to the same key, in which case one set inherits the other's eligibility verdict and the returned counts are silently wrong (either inflated or not upsampled). Since this cache is shared across processes, the wrong value is served broadly. Serialize the sorted ids (or a stable digest with low collision risk) into the key instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same problematic line of code—using Python's built-in `hash()` to construct a shared cache key—and both recommend the same fix (serializing the sorted `project_ids` deterministically into the key). Although the candidate focuses on 64-bit hash collisions while the golden comment focuses on cross-process non-determinism (though Python's `hash()` on tuples of integers is actually deterministic across processes, making the candidate's reasoning arguably more technically accurate alongside the shared recommendation for a stable serialization), they point to the exact same design flaw and remediation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `discover` for the errors-only/transactions-only probe queries) while the outer `dataset` is still the originally requested one (e.g. `metrics_enhanced_performance`). As a result the upsampling decision is computed for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling is silently skipped for the split errors query (under-reported counts for allowlisted projects) and could conversely be applied to a dataset whose query builder has no `upsampled_count` function. The check should use `scoped_dataset`.

`upsampled_count()` only registered for the discover dataset, but applied to the errors dataset

`upsampled_count` is added only to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter`, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` returns `True` unconditionally when `dataset is sentry.snuba.errors`. The errors dataset is resolved through its own `ErrorsDatasetConfig` function registry, which does not contain `upsampled_count`, so any `yAxis=count()` request with `dataset=errors` for allowlisted projects will be rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` and then fail with an "is not a valid function" search error instead of returning data. There is also no test exercising `dataset=errors`, so this path is completely uncovered.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated error queries

`_is_error_focused_query` does `"event.type:error" in query`. This matches `!event.type:error` (a query that explicitly excludes errors, i.e. transactions) as well as occurrences inside quoted free-text/message filters. For such queries the discover `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (`sum(sample_weight)`), producing wrong (or null/zero) numbers for non-error rows where `sample_weight` is absent. The check needs to parse the query (or at least exclude negations) rather than do a raw substring test.

Error-focus detection reads `request.GET['query']` instead of the query actually executed

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` / `_is_error_focused_query` inspect the raw `request.GET["query"]`, but `_get_event_stats` is frequently called with a *modified* query string: the dashboard widget split path builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (errors-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transactions-only). Because the helper never sees these, the errors-only probe query is not recognized as error-focused (upsampling skipped, counts under-reported) while the transactions-only query inherits the decision made from the original request. The query string that is actually executed should be passed into the helper.

60s eligibility cache has no working invalidation; option changes are ignored and the cache adds little value

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds keyed by org + project ids. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to clear it but is never called from anywhere in the codebase, and it requires knowing the exact project-id set used in the cache key, so it cannot realistically invalidate all affected entries when `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes. Consequence: adding or (more importantly) removing a project from the allowlist — e.g. to stop emitting inflated counts during an incident — takes effect only after up to 60s, with no way to force it. Note also that `options.get` is already backed by the options cache, so the extra caching layer buys little while introducing this staleness and a stale-data risk. The surrounding docstring claiming "we always have the latest configuration state" contradicts the caching behaviour.

Two problems with the new `upsampled_count` SnQL function: (1) `sample_weight` is not guaranteed to be populated for all error rows in an allowlisted project (events ingested before the feature was enabled, or SDKs not sending `contexts.error_sampling`); for a nullable column ClickHouse `sum` over all-NULL rows returns NULL, and `toInt64` of that stays NULL, so the timeseries can return `null` counts where consumers (zerofill, frontend charts, alert comparisons) expect integers. The docstring's assumption that "sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects" is not enforced anywhere — consider `ifNull(...)`/`sumIf` semantics. (2) Unlike the neighbouring internal helpers, it is not marked `private=True`, so any user can request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover for non-allowlisted projects and get meaningless zero/null results, a new public API surface that was presumably not intended.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` injects `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` from `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` in `store_event`, bypassing the real ingest path (relay/event manager) that is responsible for deriving the sampling weight in production. The new endpoint tests therefore validate upsampled counts against a value the test harness itself invents, so a regression in the real normalization/ingest logic would not be caught. Additionally both `try/except Exception: pass` blocks hide genuine problems (e.g. a non-numeric `client_sample_rate`), silently producing events without a sample rate and turning a meaningful assertion failure into a confusing count mismatch.

The PR adds a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`) at path `sentry-repo` with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local tooling: it pollutes the repository tree, makes `git submodule status/update` and some clone/CI tooling report errors for an unregistered submodule, and pins a commit of the repository inside itself. It should be removed from the PR.

`assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` (and the following line) claim the bucket contains 1 event while asserting a count of 10. The value 10 is the upsampled count (1 event at a 0.1 client sample rate); the comment makes the assertion look wrong and will mislead the next person debugging a failure here. State that the raw event count is 1 and the expected upsampled count is 10.

In the new `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user after `self.login_as(user=self.user)`, so `self.user` no longer refers to the authenticated user; any later use of `self.user` for auth assertions in this class would be wrong (the workaround `self.authed_user` hints at the confusion). The class also lacks tests for the two riskiest new behaviours: requests with `dataset=errors` (where `upsampled_count()` is applied unconditionally) and the newly added 60-second eligibility cache (stale allowlist results), both of which are currently unverified.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every non-granting cached check now triggers a full DB permission re-query

`getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` no longer short-circuit on the permission cache (the cache lookups were removed), and `Check` only returns early when the cached permissions grant access. Consequently every Check for a resource the user is not (yet) known to have access to performs the full store path again (basic role, teams, `GetUserPermissions`) instead of being served from the 30s cache. The denial cache only bounds this per (action, name, folder) tuple, so workloads that check many distinct objects (e.g. per-item authorization over a large dashboard set) will issue one permission query per object per TTL, a large increase in DB load compared to the previous behaviour. Consider limiting the DB fallback (e.g. only when the cached entry is older than a short grace period, or once per user/action per interval).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the exact same code behavior (Check trusts cached grants and returns early, while cached denials bypass the cache and trigger a fresh DB lookup), though the golden comment frames the concern around the security risk of trusting stale grants while the candidate frames it around the performance impact of ignoring cached denials. Since they point to the exact same asymmetric caching mechanism in the code, it is a match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually exercise the short-circuit and its comment is wrong

In "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permission cache is seeded with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. not allowed. Additionally `s.store`/`s.permissionStore` are the default empty `fakeStore`, which returns no permissions. The assertion `resp.Allowed == false` therefore holds even if the denial cache were ignored entirely, so the test gives no coverage of the new early-return path. Seed the permission cache with `true` (and/or a store that grants access) so the test fails if the denial cache is not consulted.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug in the test: the comment states that cached permissions allow access, while the map actually stores `false` for `dashboards:uid:dash1` instead of `true`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key can collide across different resources (underscore delimiter)

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user UID, action, resource name and parent folder with `_` as the only separator. Resource names and folder UIDs in Grafana may legally contain underscores, so distinct checks produce identical keys, e.g. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") both yield `...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. Because `Check` now returns an immediate deny on a key hit (service.go:117), a legitimate deny for one resource will spuriously deny access to a different resource for the whole 30s TTL, with no way for the caller to recover. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or hash/length-prefix the components.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys using underscores as delimiters, which can lead to key collisions when the components themselves contain underscores, resulting in false permission denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial is cached even when the deny came from a stale folder tree, stacking staleness

When the cached permissions do not grant access, the code re-queries permissions from the DB, but `checkInheritedPermissions`/`buildFolderTree` still use the 30s-cached folder tree (service.go:609-635). If the folder tree is stale and does not yet contain a freshly created parent folder, the check denies and that deny is then stored in `permDenialCache` for another full TTL. The staleness windows add up (up to ~2x shortCacheTTL), so a user who just created a nested folder/dashboard can keep being denied even after the permission refresh - exactly the scenario this PR aims to fix. Either bypass/refresh the folder tree on the fallback path, or do not cache denials that were produced by an inherited-permission lookup against a cached tree.

Denial cache has unbounded key cardinality (one entry per user/action/name/folder)

The denial cache key includes the requested resource name and parent folder, so the number of entries grows with the number of distinct objects ever denied, per user and action. With a local in-memory cache that has no size limit (see `cache.NewLocalCache` in pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:88), a user or service scanning many resources they cannot access (thousands of dashboards) will populate thousands of entries within each 30s window, which can translate into significant memory pressure on large instances. A bounded/LRU cache or a coarser key is needed.

permissionCacheUsage metric is now misleading

`permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with "true" on a denial-cache hit (line 118), mixing two different caches into one hit-rate metric, and it is incremented with "false" at line 137 even when the permission cache was actually hit but simply did not grant access. The resulting cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts for the permission cache will report wrong values. Use a separate label/metric for the denial cache and only report "false" on a real permission-cache miss.

Denial key uses raw subject UID while permission key uses resolved UID

The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw subject identifier from the request), whereas `userPermCacheKey` is built from `userIdentifiers.UID` resolved via `GetUserIdentifiers` (which treats numeric subjects as internal IDs). For a subject passed as `user:<numeric id>` the two caches are keyed on different identifiers, so the same user gets duplicate/independent denial entries depending on the subject form used by the caller, and denial entries cannot be reasoned about together with the permission entries. Resolve identifiers first and key both caches on the same resolved UID.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a constant pipeline signature, not a per-request nonce

The OAuth2 authorize request is sent with `state = pipeline.signature`, and the callback validates `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic hash of the pipeline's view classes: it is identical for every user, every org and every installation attempt (the tests hard-code `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and reuse it across different users/orgs), and it is exposed in plaintext in every authorize redirect URL. A constant, publicly known value provides no CSRF/code-injection protection, contrary to the PR description's claim that a `state` mismatch is a security check: an attacker can craft `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker code>&state=9cae...` and have the victim's pipeline exchange the attacker's code and bind the attacker's GitHub login into `github_authenticated_user`. Follow the pattern in `OAuth2LoginView`/`OAuth2CallbackView`: generate a random nonce (`secrets.token_hex()`), `pipeline.bind_state("state", nonce)`, and compare the callback value against the stored nonce.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same security vulnerability as the golden comment: using the static/constant `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth `state` parameter instead of generating a random, per-request value (nonce).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unguarded `metadata["sender"]["login"]` access raises KeyError/TypeError

`GitHubInstallation.dispatch` compares the pipeline state against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with direct subscript access. `sender` is only present in an Integration's metadata when the row was written by the `installation` webhook handler; `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` only adds it when `state.get("sender")` is set (it never is in this pipeline), and the pipeline's `update_or_create` overwrites the metadata on every successful install (see `test_basic_flow`, where the stored metadata has no `sender` key). So any Integration that was last written by the pipeline, and reaches this branch (Integration row exists and is ACTIVE but has no OrganizationIntegration rows, e.g. after the org integration was removed), will raise an unhandled `KeyError` here and return a 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly whether a missing sender should fail closed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` directly without checking if the `sender` key exists, which causes a `KeyError` when the sender metadata was not populated.

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user validation is skipped entirely when no Integration row exists yet

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the view immediately calls `pipeline.next_step()`, so the new `github_authenticated_user` vs. installation-sender check is never performed and `build_integration` will happily claim the installation. This is the common case for any installation whose `installation` webhook has not been processed yet (the browser redirect and the webhook race each other on every fresh install) and for installations that still exist on GitHub after the Sentry-side Integration row was deleted. Since GitHub installation ids are small sequential integers, an attacker can supply someone else's `installation_id` and, if no Integration row is present, bind that installation (and its repository access) to their own Sentry org — exactly the attack this PR aims to prevent. The sender/owner should be verified against data fetched from GitHub (e.g. the installation's account/owner via `get_installation_info`) rather than only against a pre-existing local row.

`get_user_info` failures propagate as a 500 instead of the installation-failed page

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called without a try/except. Consider loading into a local variable outside the lock and only taking the lock to publish the result.

Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled when the handler returns

All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine and build the goroutine's context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the inbound apiserver request context. net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which typically happens before/while the goroutine runs. The legacy store call therefore receives an already-cancelled context and its DB work will be aborted, so the "safe measure" legacy write silently never happens for most requests, leaving legacy storage permanently out of sync. The goroutine must detach from the request context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context carrying only the needed values) before applying the timeout.

Legacy write errors in goroutines are swallowed with no logging

In Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) the error returned by the legacy store is only used as a boolean for the duration metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since the caller has already received a success response, a failed legacy write now produces no error, no log line and no retry — divergence between unified and legacy storage becomes undiagnosable. Log the error (with name/kind) in each goroutine.

Goroutines have no panic recovery; a legacy store panic crashes the process

The four goroutines spawned in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection call into legacy storage without a `defer recover()`. Synchronous calls were previously protected by the apiserver's per-request panic handler; a panic on a bare goroutine terminates the whole Grafana process. Any panic in a legacy store (e.g. nil map/SQL layer bug) is now fatal instead of a 500 for one request. Add recovery (and log) around the goroutine body.

Create failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. No legacy call happened, so the legacy error/duration metric is polluted with storage failures and the storage failure itself is never recorded in the storage metric. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Update failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error

On `d.Storage.Update` failure the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, but the failing call was the unified storage one and no legacy call was made. The legacy error metric is inflated with storage errors and storage failures are not counted, which will make the dual-writer dashboards misattribute failures. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object produced by unified storage

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo (`&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) so legacy storage persisted exactly the object unified storage had written. Now the original `objInfo` is replayed against the legacy store. For PATCH/apply requests the transformation is recomputed against the legacy copy, and for requests carrying a resourceVersion precondition the version comes from unified storage, which does not match the legacy row's version — legacy updates will fail with conflicts or write a different object than unified storage, silently diverging the two stores.

`d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs on a goroutine with the same `obj` pointer that was handed to `d.Storage.Create`. The generic registry store mutates the input object in place (name generation, resourceVersion, UID, creationTimestamp) and typically returns that same pointer as `created`, which the apiserver serializes into the HTTP response after this function returns. The legacy store also mutates the object it is given. Two goroutines therefore read/write the same object without synchronization — a genuine data race that can corrupt the response body or the persisted legacy record. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine.

Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write

Every mode-3 write test (Create line 63, Delete line 228, DeleteCollection line 282, Update line 343) returns as soon as the dual writer returns, with no synchronization on the goroutine that performs the legacy write and no assertion that the legacy store was called. The core behaviour this PR introduces — "write to unified storage, then asynchronously write to legacy" — is untested; the context-cancellation bug above would not be caught. In addition, because legacy and storage share a single `mock.Mock`, a legacy call cannot be distinguished from a storage call, and the goroutine can still be running (touching the mock) after the subtest finishes, which can race with test teardown. Use separate mocks per store plus a channel/WaitGroup (or `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting) to assert the legacy call happened.

The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...`, which already exists a couple of lines above, and adds hashes for modules (azure sdk, prometheus-alertmanager, old otel sdk/metric v0.39.0, otlp protos) that are unrelated to this change. The new component drops the `returnTo` parameter, so navigating from the rule list into a rule detail page loses the "return to previous" affordance that the rest of the alerting UI relies on.

Test asserts exactly 4 menu items, codifying the loss of Delete/Pause actions

The test grants `AlertingRuleDelete` and `AlertingRuleUpdate` both globally and on the folder, yet asserts `menuItems.length === 4` and never uses the newly declared `ui.menuItems.delete` selector. Because the menu still requires a ruler rule for Delete and Pause (AlertRuleMenu lines 123/165), those items are absent — and this assertion now locks that regression in, so a future fix restoring Delete/Pause would break the test instead of the test catching the missing actions. The test should explicitly assert the expected presence of Delete and Pause for a user with those permissions.

New `provenance` field on GrafanaPromRuleDTO is untested and unverified against the API

`provenance?: string` is added to `GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase` and is now the only signal used by `isProvisionedPromRule` / `GrafanaRuleListItem`'s `isProvisioned` and by the ability hooks to block editing of provisioned rules in the list view. No test (including the new `rulerRuleToPromRule` helper in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx) sets this field, so if the Grafana Prometheus rules endpoint does not return `provenance`, provisioned rules will be rendered as editable/deletable in the list view and nothing will catch it.

`logWarning` called from the render phase

`getEditableIdentifier` is invoked during render and calls `logWarning(...)` as a side effect when no identifier can be derived. Render-phase side effects run on every re-render (and twice per render under React StrictMode), so a single rule whose identifier cannot be constructed will repeatedly emit the same analytics warning. This should be moved into an effect or deduplicated.

Stale comment and variable name after removing the ruler prefetch

The ruler `getGrafanaRulerGroup` prefetch was removed, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX ... doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded" and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Both now describe behaviour that no longer exists and will mislead readers about what this block does.

Queries are now interpolated twice (ad hoc filters applied twice) per sub-request

`runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` up-front, but the sub-requests built from these targets are still executed with `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)`, and `runQuery` delegates to `DataSourceWithBackend.query()`, which maps every target through `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` again (the sub-request keeps `scopedVars` and `filters` from the original request). Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent in one respect: it calls `addAdHocFilters(target.expr, adhocFilters)`, so the same ad hoc filters are injected a second time into an expression that already contains them, yielding duplicated matchers/label filters (e.g. `{a="b", env="prod", env="prod"}` or a repeated `| env="prod"`). Variable values are also substituted twice, so any value that itself contains `$name`/`${name}` will be expanded on the second pass. Either strip `filters`/`scopedVars` from the sub-requests, or keep interpolation in a single place.

Shard path interpolates each query three times and changes the selector used to fetch shard values

`runShardSplitQuery` now interpolates targets with `applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`; the resulting sharded sub-request is then handed to `runSplitQuery()`, which (after this PR) interpolates again, and finally `datasource.runQuery()` -> `DataSourceWithBackend.query()` interpolates a third time. Since Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` re-runs `addAdHocFilters`, each pass re-inserts the same ad hoc filters into the already sharded expression, producing duplicated matchers. Additionally, the previous code called `interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars)` without ad hoc filters, whereas the new call passes `request.filters`; the selector derived by `getSelectorForShardValues()` and sent to `fetchLabelValues('__stream_shard__', { streamSelector })` now includes ad hoc filters, which silently changes which shard values are discovered. This behaviour change is untested.

Test encodes repeated interpolation (5 calls for 1 target) as expected behaviour

The assertion was changed from `interpolateVariablesInQueries` being called once to `applyTemplateVariables` being called 5 times for a single target. Those 5 calls are 1 call in `runShardSplitQuery` plus 1 per shard sub-request from the newly added interpolation inside `runSplitQuery`; i.e. the test now locks in the duplicate interpolation of each sub-request. It only passes because the mock at line 56 mutates the query object and does a plain `replace('$SELECTOR', ...)`, which is a no-op on the second pass; a realistic mock (returning a copy and re-applying ad hoc filters) would show duplicated filters. The mock also mutates its input, unlike the real `applyTemplateVariables`, which returns a new object, so target mutation regressions cannot be caught here.

New interpolation test mocks replace() in a way that contradicts real `$__auto` handling

The test's `replace` mock substitutes `$__auto` with `5m`, and the test then asserts the executed expr is `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])`. Loki's real `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately removes `__auto`, `__interval`, `__range` (and their variants) from `scopedVars` so that they are interpolated on the backend with the *split* time range; a real `templateSrv.replace` would leave `$__auto` untouched here. The test therefore asserts behaviour that does not occur in production and would not catch a regression where `$__auto` is prematurely resolved against the full range. Using a non-range variable (like the `$step` part of the test) or a real templateSrv stub with defined variables would make the test meaningful.
