Queue pool is owned by the factory but shut down by the strategy, breaking the consumer after the first rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared via `self.queue_pool`, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (queue_consumer.py lines 335-342), which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. Arroyo closes the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on assignment. The second strategy therefore gets a pool whose worker threads have exited and whose queues are shut down, so every `work_queue.put(...)` raises `queue.ShutDown`. That exception is swallowed by the `except Exception` block in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, which then marks the offset as added *and* completed - so messages are silently dropped and their offsets committed. After the first rebalance the consumer stops doing any work while continuing to advance offsets, i.e. permanent data loss. The pool must be created per strategy (or not shut down in `close()`).

Queues are unbounded and submit never applies backpressure

`queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize` and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever blocks or rejects: if the result processor is slower than the incoming message rate, arroyo will keep reading from Kafka and the strategy will buffer the entire backlog (decoded results plus the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload` kept on `WorkItem.message`) in memory until the process OOMs. Give the queues a bounded size and raise `MessageRejected` (or block) when full, and fix the docstring.

close()/join() do not drain queues or perform a final commit

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and just calls `close()`; `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread and then shuts down the pool. Because `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues, each worker exits after finishing at most one more item, so all still-queued work items are discarded. Additionally no commit is attempted after the workers stop, so offsets for items that completed since the last 1-second commit tick are never committed. Arroyo's contract for `join(timeout)` is to flush outstanding work and commit before returning; as written every shutdown/rebalance drops in-flight work and re-reads a window of messages (duplicate processing) on restart.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `Commit` callback. That callback mutates the StreamProcessor's staged-offset state and the underlying consumer, which the main poll thread is using concurrently; arroyo's consumer/commit path is not documented as thread-safe. This can corrupt the staged offset bookkeeping or raise (e.g. committing offsets for a partition that was just revoked), and the only handling is a broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` that will then spin once per second. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread (e.g. via a thread-safe queue drained in `poll()`), which is also where arroyo expects commits to happen.

OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition reassignment

`OffsetTracker` is owned by the long-lived `FixedQueuePool` and keeps `last_committed`, `all_offsets`, `outstanding` and `partition_locks` for every partition it has ever seen. On rebalance a new strategy is created but the tracker still holds the old `last_committed` values; if a partition is reassigned and the consumer must restart from an earlier offset (or the partition is assigned to another consumer and later returned), `get_committable_offsets()` will refuse to return anything `<= last_committed`, permanently stalling commits for that partition. Entries for revoked partitions are also never dropped, so the dicts grow for the lifetime of the process.

Any offset that is never submitted permanently stalls commits for the partition

`get_committable_offsets()` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and breaks as soon as an offset is not present in `all_offsets`. Offsets can be missing for reasons other than slow processing: arroyo can hand the strategy messages whose `value` is not a `BrokerValue` (the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` fails and the `except` branch then also skips recording because of the same `isinstance` check), transaction/control markers consume offsets on some topics, and anything that throws before `add_offset` leaves a hole. Once a hole exists the partition can never advance: no offsets are ever committed again, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and on restart the whole backlog is reprocessed. Track a per-partition "next expected" watermark from the messages actually received rather than requiring offset contiguity.

Failed work items are marked complete, so failures are committed and lost

`complete_offset()` is called in the `finally` block of the worker, so a work item whose `result_processor` raised is treated exactly like a successfully processed one: its offset becomes committable and is committed, with only a log line. There is no retry, no DLQ and no metric, so a transient failure (e.g. a DB hiccup) silently drops the check result. If this at-most-once behaviour is intended it should at least emit a failure metric; otherwise the offset should not be completed on error.

Kafka integration test relies on private arroyo APIs, wall-clock sleeps and a second consumer in the same group

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest` drives the consumer with `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice), busy-loops for a fixed 5 wall-clock seconds and then asserts an exact committed offset of 5 - this depends on the background commit thread and ONCE_PER_SECOND policy firing within that window, so it will flake on a loaded CI machine. It also creates a second `confluent_kafka.Consumer` with the same `group.id` to read committed offsets, which joins the group and can trigger a rebalance/return stale offsets, and `verify_consumer.committed(partitions)` is called without a timeout so it can block indefinitely.

Per-message gauge emitted from every worker with identical tags

Every processed item emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` as a gauge tagged only with `identifier`. All N workers report their own queue's depth under the same metric name and tag set, so the values overwrite each other and the resulting series is meaningless, while the emission rate equals the message rate. Either tag by `worker_id`/queue index or report queue depth periodically from `poll()` instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative slice start on a Django QuerySet raises ValueError, not "handled automatically"

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django explicitly rejects this: `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. Since `Cursor.from_string` happily parses a negative offset from the user-supplied `cursor` query parameter, a request like `?optimized_pagination=true&cursor=0:-5:0` produces an unhandled exception / 500 rather than a 400. The inline comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` like `OffsetPaginator` does.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result passes a negative cursor.offset directly into queryset slicing when advanced features are enabled, which Django rejects with ValueError rather than handling automatically.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now silently clamps negative cursor offsets, producing inconsistent cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the behavior of every paginator derived from `BasePaginator` (issues, audit logs, many list endpoints). Previously a negative offset in a client-supplied cursor surfaced as an error from the ORM; now the query silently starts at row 0 while `build_cursor` is still handed the original negative `cursor.offset`. `_build_next_values` then computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the negative value and `_build_prev_values` treats the negative offset as "has_prev", so the returned next/prev cursors point at positions that do not correspond to the rows actually returned, causing skipped or duplicated rows on subsequent pages. Negative offsets should be rejected explicitly rather than clamped.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments target the same BasePaginator.get_result() line where cursor.is_prev leaves start_offset unclamped, so a negative cursor offset is not rejected and produces incorrect pagination/cursor behavior. The candidate describes the same bug and its consequences, despite different wording.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is numeric-keyed but is used with the `datetime` column

The endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"` to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and whose `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor integer. `AuditLogEntry.datetime` is a `datetime`, so `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`, and a cursor value would be compared against a timestamp column as a bare integer in the generated `WHERE` clause. Any request with `?optimized_pagination=true` from an authorized user will therefore fail with a 500 instead of returning a page. Date-keyed querysets require `DateTimePaginator`-style key handling (the `multiplier` conversion).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator is used with order_by='-datetime', and get_item_key applies math.floor to a datetime, raising TypeError. Extra details about cursor comparison do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
`organization_context.member` can be None, causing a 500 on every audit-log request

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the requester is not an organization member (e.g. org auth token / integration token auth, or a staff/superuser request that resolves no membership). Because `request.user.is_superuser` is `False` for non-user auth (and `AnonymousUser`), the second operand is evaluated and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working endpoint into a 500 for those auth paths. The flag should only be computed inside the `optimized_pagination` branch and must null-check `member`.

Prev-page trimming uses raw offset instead of the slice start

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the extra-row trim condition `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` uses the raw `cursor.offset`, while the rows were fetched with `start_offset` (which may differ, e.g. clamped to 0 or negative). When `offset` is negative the comparison can never be true (or is true for the wrong row count), so the extra look-behind row fetched for `is_prev` cursors is not dropped and leaks into the returned page, duplicating a row the client already saw. The condition should compare against `start_offset + limit + extra`.

Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000` and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unannounced 10x reduction in the maximum redirect-chain depth: traces whose parent/child redirect chains exceed 1000 hops will stop resolving to the correct `set_key`, so their spans get split across multiple segments and are emitted as separate (incorrect) segments. If the reduction is intentional it should be stated in the PR and the caveat comment kept; otherwise the original bound should be restored.

Eviction silently drops spans with a hardcoded limit and no metric/log

`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` trims segments to a hardcoded 1000 spans. Two problems: (1) the limit is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is the configured value and is no longer used anywhere, so the setting has no effect and the two numbers disagree; (2) the previous code path in `_load_segment_data` that dropped oversized segments emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and `logger.error`, and that observability was removed in this PR. Now span data is discarded with no metric, log, or configuration, making truncated segments undetectable in production.

zunionstore uses the default SUM aggregate, corrupting span timestamps/scores

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. The scores are `end_timestamp_precise` values used to order spans for eviction. If the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a redelivered/duplicated span that landed under a different key before the redirect was established), its score becomes the sum of two ~1.7e9 timestamps, making it the newest member forever and causing `zpopmin` to evict legitimate newer spans instead. The merges should specify `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) to preserve timestamp semantics.

`max_segment_spans` is now dead configuration

The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere; the effective limit is the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua`. Callers that set this parameter will silently get no behavior change. Either wire the value through to the Lua script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

Module docstring still describes Redis sets after the switch to sorted sets

The storage layout changed from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`) scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are now evicted at insert time when a segment exceeds the limit. The docstring (step 3 "Add the ingested span's payload to the set under `set_key`" and the glossary entry "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes plain sets and says nothing about scoring or eviction, so readers will have the wrong mental model of the key types and of the fact that spans can be dropped.

No test for the new insert-time eviction behavior

The headline change of this PR is eviction during insert (`zpopmin` once a segment exceeds 1000 spans) plus the set→sorted-set migration, but no test exercises a segment larger than the limit. Existing tests only cover 4-5 span segments, so neither the trimming threshold, the choice of which spans are discarded (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`), nor the removal of the old `max_segment_spans` guard in `_load_segment_data` is verified. A regression in the Lua arithmetic (e.g. off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`, or the `span_count == 0` fallback) would go unnoticed.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator has no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` is a new public paginator with non-trivial branching (negative-offset path, prev-cursor extra-row trimming, `enable_advanced_features` flag) and it is already wired into a production endpoint, yet no tests are added for it or for the audit-log endpoint's new `optimized_pagination` code path. The datetime/negative-slice failures in this class would have been caught by a single test.

Misleading comment claims a behavior change that was not made

The added comment says "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`, but no code changed here — `Cursor` always accepted negative offsets, and callers (e.g. `OffsetPaginator`) are the ones that validate them. The comment implies `Cursor` now intentionally supports negative offsets as a feature, which will mislead future readers into assuming downstream paginators handle them safely (they do not; Django rejects negative slice starts).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key built from Python `hash()` of project ids can collide

The cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}"`. Using an opaque 64-bit hash instead of the sorted ids themselves means two different project sets in the same organization can map to the same key, in which case one set inherits the other's eligibility verdict and the returned counts are silently wrong (either inflated or not upsampled). Since this cache is shared across processes, the wrong value is served broadly. Serialize the sorted ids (or a stable digest with low collision risk) into the key instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments target the same cache-key construction using Python hash() over project IDs and recommend replacing it with deterministic serialization. The candidate emphasizes collision risk rather than cross-process hash randomization, but it identifies the same underlying code issue and fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first argument, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(...)`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `discover` for the errors-only/transactions-only probe queries) while the outer `dataset` is still the originally requested one (e.g. `metrics_enhanced_performance`). As a result the upsampling decision is computed for a dataset that is not the one being queried: upsampling is silently skipped for the split errors query (under-reported counts for allowlisted projects) and could conversely be applied to a dataset whose query builder has no `upsampled_count` function. The check should use `scoped_dataset`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, so in dashboard split paths (querying discover while the original dataset is metrics) upsampling is skipped for allowlisted projects. The candidate adds extra detail but points to the identical issue.

false_positives.candidate:
`upsampled_count()` only registered for the discover dataset, but applied to the errors dataset

`upsampled_count` is added only to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter`, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` returns `True` unconditionally when `dataset is sentry.snuba.errors`. The errors dataset is resolved through its own `ErrorsDatasetConfig` function registry, which does not contain `upsampled_count`, so any `yAxis=count()` request with `dataset=errors` for allowlisted projects will be rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count` and then fail with an "is not a valid function" search error instead of returning data. There is also no test exercising `dataset=errors`, so this path is completely uncovered.

`_is_error_focused_query` substring match also matches negated error queries

`_is_error_focused_query` does `"event.type:error" in query`. This matches `!event.type:error` (a query that explicitly excludes errors, i.e. transactions) as well as occurrences inside quoted free-text/message filters. For such queries the discover `count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (`sum(sample_weight)`), producing wrong (or null/zero) numbers for non-error rows where `sample_weight` is absent. The check needs to parse the query (or at least exclude negations) rather than do a raw substring test.

Error-focus detection reads `request.GET['query']` instead of the query actually executed

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` / `_is_error_focused_query` inspect the raw `request.GET["query"]`, but `_get_event_stats` is frequently called with a *modified* query string: the dashboard widget split path builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (errors-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transactions-only). Because the helper never sees these, the errors-only probe query is not recognized as error-focused (upsampling skipped, counts under-reported) while the transactions-only query inherits the decision made from the original request. The query string that is actually executed should be passed into the helper.

60s eligibility cache has no working invalidation; option changes are ignored and the cache adds little value

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist decision for 60 seconds keyed by org + project ids. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to clear it but is never called from anywhere in the codebase, and it requires knowing the exact project-id set used in the cache key, so it cannot realistically invalidate all affected entries when `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` changes. Consequence: adding or (more importantly) removing a project from the allowlist — e.g. to stop emitting inflated counts during an incident — takes effect only after up to 60s, with no way to force it. Note also that `options.get` is already backed by the options cache, so the extra caching layer buys little while introducing this staleness and a stale-data risk. The surrounding docstring claiming "we always have the latest configuration state" contradicts the caching behaviour.

`toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` can yield NULL and is exposed as a public function

Two problems with the new `upsampled_count` SnQL function: (1) `sample_weight` is not guaranteed to be populated for all error rows in an allowlisted project (events ingested before the feature was enabled, or SDKs not sending `contexts.error_sampling`); for a nullable column ClickHouse `sum` over all-NULL rows returns NULL, and `toInt64` of that stays NULL, so the timeseries can return `null` counts where consumers (zerofill, frontend charts, alert comparisons) expect integers. The docstring's assumption that "sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects" is not enforced anywhere — consider `ifNull(...)`/`sumIf` semantics. (2) Unlike the neighbouring internal helpers, it is not marked `private=True`, so any user can request `yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover for non-allowlisted projects and get meaningless zero/null results, a new public API surface that was presumably not intended.

Test factory fabricates `sample_rate` and silently swallows all errors

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` injects `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` from `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` in `store_event`, bypassing the real ingest path (relay/event manager) that is responsible for deriving the sampling weight in production. The new endpoint tests therefore validate upsampled counts against a value the test harness itself invents, so a regression in the real normalization/ingest logic would not be caught. Additionally both `try/except Exception: pass` blocks hide genuine problems (e.g. a non-numeric `client_sample_rate`), silently producing events without a sample rate and turning a meaningful assertion failure into a confusing count mismatch.

Stray git submodule entry `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909...`) at path `sentry-repo` with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly an accidental artifact of local tooling: it pollutes the repository tree, makes `git submodule status/update` and some clone/CI tooling report errors for an unregistered submodule, and pins a commit of the repository inside itself. It should be removed from the PR.

Misleading comments on upsampled count assertions

`assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` (and the following line) claim the bucket contains 1 event while asserting a count of 10. The value 10 is the upsampled count (1 event at a 0.1 client sample rate); the comment makes the assertion look wrong and will mislead the next person debugging a failure here. State that the raw event count is 1 and the expected upsampled count is 10.

`setUp` overwrites `self.user` after `login_as`, and no coverage for errors dataset / caching

In the new `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user after `self.login_as(user=self.user)`, so `self.user` no longer refers to the authenticated user; any later use of `self.user` for auth assertions in this class would be wrong (the workaround `self.authed_user` hints at the confusion). The class also lacks tests for the two riskiest new behaviours: requests with `dataset=errors` (where `upsampled_count()` is applied unconditionally) and the newly added 60-second eligibility cache (stale allowlist results), both of which are currently unverified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every non-granting cached check now triggers a full DB permission re-query

`getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` no longer short-circuit on the permission cache (the cache lookups were removed), and `Check` only returns early when the cached permissions grant access. Consequently every Check for a resource the user is not (yet) known to have access to performs the full store path again (basic role, teams, `GetUserPermissions`) instead of being served from the 30s cache. The denial cache only bounds this per (action, name, folder) tuple, so workloads that check many distinct objects (e.g. per-item authorization over a large dashboard set) will issue one permission query per object per TTL, a large increase in DB load compared to the previous behaviour. Consider limiting the DB fallback (e.g. only when the cached entry is older than a short grace period, or once per user/action per interval).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same asymmetric permission-cache logic: cached grants short-circuit Check, while cached denials do not and trigger a fresh DB lookup. The candidate emphasizes the resulting DB load rather than the stale-grant security risk, but the underlying code issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually exercise the short-circuit and its comment is wrong

In "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permission cache is seeded with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. not allowed. Additionally `s.store`/`s.permissionStore` are the default empty `fakeStore`, which returns no permissions. The assertion `resp.Allowed == false` therefore holds even if the denial cache were ignored entirely, so the test gives no coverage of the new early-return path. Seed the permission cache with `true` (and/or a store that grants access) so the test fails if the denial cache is not consulted.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same test bug: the comment claims the cached permission allows access, but the seeded map value is false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so the denial path is not actually proven. The extra coverage explanation is consistent with that issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key can collide across different resources (underscore delimiter)

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user UID, action, resource name and parent folder with `_` as the only separator. Resource names and folder UIDs in Grafana may legally contain underscores, so distinct checks produce identical keys, e.g. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") both yield `...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. Because `Check` now returns an immediate deny on a key hit (service.go:117), a legitimate deny for one resource will spuriously deny access to a different resource for the whole 30s TTL, with no way for the caller to recover. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or hash/length-prefix the components.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in userPermDenialCacheKey: underscore-delimited concatenation creates ambiguous/colliding cache keys when components contain underscores, causing incorrect denial cache hits and spurious permission denials.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial is cached even when the deny came from a stale folder tree, stacking staleness

When the cached permissions do not grant access, the code re-queries permissions from the DB, but `checkInheritedPermissions`/`buildFolderTree` still use the 30s-cached folder tree (service.go:609-635). If the folder tree is stale and does not yet contain a freshly created parent folder, the check denies and that deny is then stored in `permDenialCache` for another full TTL. The staleness windows add up (up to ~2x shortCacheTTL), so a user who just created a nested folder/dashboard can keep being denied even after the permission refresh - exactly the scenario this PR aims to fix. Either bypass/refresh the folder tree on the fallback path, or do not cache denials that were produced by an inherited-permission lookup against a cached tree.

Denial cache has unbounded key cardinality (one entry per user/action/name/folder)

The denial cache key includes the requested resource name and parent folder, so the number of entries grows with the number of distinct objects ever denied, per user and action. With a local in-memory cache that has no size limit (see `cache.NewLocalCache` in pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:88), a user or service scanning many resources they cannot access (thousands of dashboards) will populate thousands of entries within each 30s window, which can translate into significant memory pressure on large instances. A bounded/LRU cache or a coarser key is needed.

permissionCacheUsage metric is now misleading

`permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with "true" on a denial-cache hit (line 118), mixing two different caches into one hit-rate metric, and it is incremented with "false" at line 137 even when the permission cache was actually hit but simply did not grant access. The resulting cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts for the permission cache will report wrong values. Use a separate label/metric for the denial cache and only report "false" on a real permission-cache miss.

Denial key uses raw subject UID while permission key uses resolved UID

The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw subject identifier from the request), whereas `userPermCacheKey` is built from `userIdentifiers.UID` resolved via `GetUserIdentifiers` (which treats numeric subjects as internal IDs). For a subject passed as `user:<numeric id>` the two caches are keyed on different identifiers, so the same user gets duplicate/independent denial entries depending on the subject form used by the caller, and denial entries cannot be reasoned about together with the permission entries. true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a constant pipeline signature, not a per-request nonce

The OAuth2 authorize request is sent with `state = pipeline.signature`, and the callback validates `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic hash of the pipeline's view classes: it is identical for every user, every org and every installation attempt (the tests hard-code `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` and reuse it across different users/orgs), and it is exposed in plaintext in every authorize redirect URL. A constant, publicly known value provides no CSRF/code-injection protection, contrary to the PR description's claim that a `state` mismatch is a security check: an attacker can craft `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker code>&state=9cae...` and have the victim's pipeline exchange the attacker's code and bind the attacker's GitHub login into `github_authenticated_user`. Follow the pattern in `OAuth2LoginView`/`OAuth2CallbackView`: generate a random nonce (`secrets.token_hex()`), `pipeline.bind_state("state", nonce)`, and compare the callback value against the stored nonce.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OAuth state is set to the static pipeline.signature instead of a per-request random nonce, so the CSRF check is ineffective. The candidate adds detail but points to the identical issue and fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unguarded `metadata["sender"]["login"]` access raises KeyError/TypeError

`GitHubInstallation.dispatch` compares the pipeline state against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with direct subscript access. `sender` is only present in an Integration's metadata when the row was written by the `installation` webhook handler; `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration` only adds it when `state.get("sender")` is set (it never is in this pipeline), and the pipeline's `update_or_create` overwrites the metadata on every successful install (see `test_basic_flow`, where the stored metadata has no `sender` key). So any Integration that was last written by the pipeline, and reaches this branch (Integration row exists and is ACTIVE but has no OrganizationIntegration rows, e.g. after the org integration was removed), will raise an unhandled `KeyError` here and return a 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly whether a missing sender should fail closed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: direct access to integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking that the sender key exists, causing an unhandled KeyError for integrations whose metadata lacks sender. The candidate adds context and a suggested fix but points to the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user validation is skipped entirely when no Integration row exists yet

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the view immediately calls `pipeline.next_step()`, so the new `github_authenticated_user` vs. installation-sender check is never performed and `build_integration` will happily claim the installation. This is the common case for any installation whose `installation` webhook has not been processed yet (the browser redirect and the webhook race each other on every fresh install) and for installations that still exist on GitHub after the Sentry-side Integration row was deleted. Since GitHub installation ids are small sequential integers, an attacker can supply someone else's `installation_id` and, if no Integration row is present, bind that installation (and its repository access) to their own Sentry org — exactly the attack this PR aims to prevent. The sender/owner should be verified against data fetched from GitHub (e.g. the installation's account/owner via `get_installation_info`) rather than only against a pre-existing local row.

`get_user_info` failures propagate as a 500 instead of the installation-failed page

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called without a try/except. It performs an HTTP request to `/user` and raises `ApiError` on non-2xx responses (revoked token, GitHub 5xx, rate limiting), and may also return a non-dict payload, which would make the following `"login" not in authenticated_user_info` check raise `TypeError`. Any of these cases yields an unhandled exception and a generic 500 in the middle of the install pipeline rather than the `error(...)` page the rest of this view uses. Wrap the call and fall back to `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path

The test still stubs `/app/installations/{id}` as 404, but the request it now makes supplies `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature used everywhere else in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore short-circuits in `OAuthLoginView`'s state check and the assertion only verifies the generic "Invalid installation request." page. The previously covered behaviour — `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` on a 404 from GitHub — is now untested, and the test name/intent is misleading. Use the correct state so the pipeline reaches `build_integration`, and assert the installation-not-found message (or add a separate test for the state-mismatch case).

No coverage for the matching-sender branch or for metadata without a sender

`test_github_user_mismatch` only covers the negative branch (authenticated login != `metadata["sender"]["login"]`). There is no test where an Integration row exists with a `sender` whose login matches the authenticated user (the branch that must let the install continue), and none where the existing Integration's metadata has no `sender` key — the latter currently crashes with a `KeyError` in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`. Both branches are reachable in production and should be asserted.

false_positives.candidate:

`cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)` only includes the realm id and the fetch mode, while the per-organization dimension is pushed into the `searchKey` of a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` entry. Consequently all organizations of a realm share one cache entry for `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`. Each time a login happens for an organization whose id is not yet in that entry, the code takes the `cached == null` branch and calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` and then re-adds a copy of the whole query object (lines 234-241). In a realm with many organizations this means (a) one cache entry that grows linearly with the number of organizations, (b) a full invalidate-and-rebuild of the shared entry on the first login of every new organization, and in a cluster nodes repeatedly discard each other's accumulated entry for different orgs. true_positives.matched_candidate:

The feature-flag lookup result is therefore completely discarded and the function is a constant `false`. Even if the intent is to hard-disable SQL expressions, this shape is dangerous: a future reader will assume the flag is honoured and the inverted condition means a one-line "re-enable" change would turn the feature on when the flag is *disabled*. It is also the kind of ineffectual assignment that staticcheck/golangci can flag and break CI. Prefer an explicit `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, or remove the helper and return the error unconditionally.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

`TablesList` builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('<rawSQL>')` by string concatenation with only naive `'` doubling and then calls `DB.RunCommands`, which the new stub in db.go always fails with `errors.New("not implemented")`. So the whole function can only ever return an error, and everything after line 26 (`tablesFromAST`, `astError`, `existsInList`, the `flatten` dependency) is unreachable. It focuses on TablesList specifically and doesn't mention QueryFramesInto, but the underlying bug is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Disabled SQL expression returns a plain error with a misleading message

When a `QueryTypeSQL` node is encountered the reader returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. Unlike the other error paths in this package (e.g. `NewSQLCommand` uses `errutil.BadRequest`), a bare error carries no status/public-message metadata, so an operator-enabled `sqlExpressions` toggle will surface as an opaque server error rather than a 400 with a clear reason. The wording is also misleading: the feature is intentionally disabled for security, not merely unimplemented, which will send users chasing a non-existent bug. Use `errutil.BadRequest` with a public message stating the feature is disabled.

No regression test asserting SQL expressions are rejected

This PR is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) that disables server-side SQL expressions, but no test is added covering either entry point: `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` with `type: sql` (should error even with `FlagSqlExpressions` enabled) and `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` (which now fails because `sql.TablesList` errors). Without such tests, a later refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` or of the `sql.DB` stub can silently re-enable the RCE/LFI path with no CI signal.

tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without a length check

`flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` will panic with an index-out-of-range if the deserialised AST JSON is an empty array (e.g. `[]`). The function is currently unreachable because `RunCommands` always errors, but if the DuckDB-backed implementation is ever restored this is an attacker-influenceable panic in a request path. Stub DB silently degrades SQLCommand.Execute into an opaque runtime error

`NewInMemoryDB()` returns a struct whose `QueryFramesInto` always returns `not implemented`. `SQLCommand.Execute` (pkg/expr/sql_command.go:100-105) assigns that to `rsp.Error` and returns a nil error, so if any code path ever reaches execution (for example a query constructed without going through `NewSQLCommand`/`ReadQuery`) the user sees a bare "not implemented" in the query result instead of a clear "SQL expressions are disabled" message. `featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions` is still registered and documented as enabling server-side SQL expressions, but after this change enabling it has no effect other than producing an error on every SQL expression query. Operators who follow the existing docs will enable the toggle and get a confusing failure. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of cache after acquiring write lock (no double-checked locking)

After the RLock fast path fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads `entryPointAssetsCache`. If N requests arrive concurrently before the cache is populated (e.g. at startup), all N will block on the write lock and each will in turn re-open and re-parse `assets-manifest.json` (and, when the CDN branch is enabled, perform an HTTP request) and overwrite the cache, even though the first one already populated it. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` would make the cache actually serve concurrent callers and avoid the redundant I/O.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same incomplete double-checked locking bug: after the read-lock fast path fails, the write-lock path does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache, so concurrent callers can redundantly repopulate the cache. The suggested post-Lock re-check matches the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocking file/network I/O performed while holding the exclusive lock

`readWebAssetsFromCDN` (HTTP GET with the request context) and `readWebAssetsFromFile` are executed while the write lock is held, so every other caller of `GetWebAssets` — including readers that would otherwise hit the cache — is blocked for the duration of a network round trip or disk read. In dev mode, where the cache is bypassed on every call, this fully serializes all asset-manifest lookups across requests. Consider loading into a local variable outside the lock and only taking the lock to publish the result.

No test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls

The PR fixes a data race but adds no test. A simple test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines (runnable under `-race`), covering both `setting.Dev` and non-dev configs, would prevent regression if the locking is later removed or the global is reintroduced elsewhere.

Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite

In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite fallback builds the `IN (...)` list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop, re-allocating and copying the whole accumulated string on each iteration. With the batch sizes this code path is designed for (the new test exercises 32767 IDs per batch), this is O(n^2) in allocations and bytes copied and runs for every batch of every cleanup cycle. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be cancelled when the handler returns

All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine and build the goroutine's context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the inbound apiserver request context. net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which typically happens before/while the goroutine runs. The legacy store call therefore receives an already-cancelled context and its DB work will be aborted, so the "safe measure" legacy write silently never happens for most requests, leaving legacy storage permanently out of sync. The goroutine must detach from the request context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context carrying only the needed values) before applying the timeout.

Legacy write errors in goroutines are swallowed with no logging

In Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) the error returned by the legacy store is only used as a boolean for the duration metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged these failures. Since the caller has already received a success response, a failed legacy write now produces no error, no log line and no retry — divergence between unified and legacy storage becomes undiagnosable. Log the error (with name/kind) in each goroutine.

Goroutines have no panic recovery; a legacy store panic crashes the process

The four goroutines spawned in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection call into legacy storage without a `defer recover()`. Synchronous calls were previously protected by the apiserver's per-request panic handler; a panic on a bare goroutine terminates the whole Grafana process. Any panic in a legacy store (e.g. nil map/SQL layer bug) is now fatal instead of a 500 for one request. Add recovery (and log) around the goroutine body.

Create failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. No legacy call happened, so the legacy error/duration metric is polluted with storage failures and the storage failure itself is never recorded in the storage metric. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Update failure path records a legacy-duration metric for a storage error

On `d.Storage.Update` failure the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, but the failing call was the unified storage one and no legacy call was made. The legacy error metric is inflated with storage errors and storage failures are not counted, which will make the dual-writer dashboards misattribute failures. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object produced by unified storage

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo (`&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) so legacy storage persisted exactly the object unified storage had written. Now the original `objInfo` is replayed against the legacy store. For PATCH/apply requests the transformation is recomputed against the legacy copy, and for requests carrying a resourceVersion precondition the version comes from unified storage, which does not match the legacy row's version — legacy updates will fail with conflicts or write a different object than unified storage, silently diverging the two stores.

Object passed to the async legacy Create may be mutated concurrently with response serialization

`d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` runs on a goroutine with the same `obj` pointer that was handed to `d.Storage.Create`. The generic registry store mutates the input object in place (name generation, resourceVersion, UID, creationTimestamp) and typically returns that same pointer as `created`, which the apiserver serializes into the HTTP response after this function returns. The legacy store also mutates the object it is given. Two goroutines therefore read/write the same object without synchronization — a genuine data race that can corrupt the response body or the persisted legacy record. Deep-copy the object before handing it to the goroutine.

Tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write

Every mode-3 write test (Create line 63, Delete line 228, DeleteCollection line 282, Update line 343) returns as soon as the dual writer returns, with no synchronization on the goroutine that performs the legacy write and no assertion that the legacy store was called. The core behaviour this PR introduces — "write to unified storage, then asynchronously write to legacy" — is untested; the context-cancellation bug above would not be caught. In addition, because legacy and storage share a single `mock.Mock`, a legacy call cannot be distinguished from a storage call, and the goroutine can still be running (touching the mock) after the subtest finishes, which can race with test teardown. Use separate mocks per store plus a channel/WaitGroup (or `mock.AssertExpectations` after waiting) to assert the legacy call happened.

go.work.sum gains a duplicate entry and unrelated dependency hashes

The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...`, which already exists a couple of lines above, and adds hashes for modules (azure sdk, prometheus-alertmanager, old otel sdk/metric v0.39.0, otlp protos) that are unrelated to this change. This looks like an accidental/mechanical `go work sync` from a different module set; it makes the dual-writer PR carry unrelated dependency churn and the duplicate line will keep reappearing/disappearing in future diffs. Revert go.work.sum unless the change is actually required to build.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-insert race allows the device limit to be exceeded

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the current device count with `CountDevices` and then, if `count < s.deviceLimit`, performs an unconditional upsert. Multiple concurrent requests (and multiple Grafana instances sharing the database) can all observe `count == limit-1` and all insert, so the number of distinct anonymous devices can exceed `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap, the count and insert need to be in a single transaction/statement (e.g. an `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) or the overshoot needs to be acknowledged as acceptable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same check-then-insert race where concurrent requests can pass the device count check and exceed the limit, and both recommend making the operation atomic via a transaction or equivalent locking/statement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected == 0 is reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached, conflating distinct conditions

`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever the UPDATE affects zero rows. Zero rows also occurs when the row exists but its `updated_at` falls outside the `[now-30d, now+1m]` window, and on MySQL an UPDATE that writes values identical to the stored ones reports 0 affected rows (the driver does not enable CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS), which can happen when `updated_at` is truncated to second precision and the same device is written twice within the same second. In those cases an already-known device is incorrectly refused authentication with a "device limit reached" error. The limit-reached condition should be distinguished from "row not updated" (e.g. check existence explicitly or treat 0 rows for a pre-existing device as success).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached, even though zero rows can mean the device is missing or outside the time window (not a limit). The candidate adds extra MySQL/precision detail but points to the same root cause and fix direction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed after the first rejection because the local cache is populated before the store write

`tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `a.localCache` (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) *before* calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the device limit is reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and `Anonymous.Authenticate` denies the request — but the key is already cached. Every subsequent request from the same device ID hits the `if _, ok := a.localCache.Get(key); ok { return nil }` early-return for the next 29 minutes, so `TagDevice` returns nil and the anonymous user is authenticated normally. The configured limit therefore only blocks a device's very first request and is effectively unenforced afterwards. The cache entry should only be set after a successful store write (and removed/not set on error).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device key before CreateOrUpdateDevice, so an ErrDeviceLimitReached response leaves the entry in place and later requests bypass the limit for the 29-minute cache lifetime.

false_positives.candidate:
New auth.anonymous.device_limit key missing from conf/defaults.ini, breaking env-var override and documentation

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` adds a new configuration key, but `conf/defaults.ini` (and `conf/sample.ini`) are not updated in this PR. Grafana applies environment-variable overrides by iterating the keys that exist in the loaded ini files, so a key that is absent from defaults.ini cannot be set via `GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT` — operators running in containers (the common case) would silently get the default of 0/unlimited. The option is also undocumented, so users have no way to discover it or its semantics (0 = unlimited).

Raw ErrDeviceLimitReached returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 500 to the user

`ErrDeviceLimitReached` is a plain `fmt.Errorf` value, and it is returned directly from `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn broker/HTTP layer has no mapping for it, so an anonymous visitor who is rejected because of the device limit receives a generic internal-server-error rather than a meaningful status/message. Use an `errutil` error with an appropriate status (e.g. 429/403) and a user-facing message so the rejection is diagnosable and does not look like a server fault.

Provider signature changes are not reflected in the DI/wire configuration

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `sqlStore db.DB` instead of `anonStore anonstore.AnonStore`, and `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. The wire configuration (pkg/server/wire.go and generated wire_gen.go), which registers `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and binds it to `anonstore.AnonStore`, is not part of this PR. Unless those files are updated, wire generation/compilation fails (no provider for `int64`, and the old call `ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore)` no longer matches). Also, because the store is now constructed inside the service, the previously injectable `anonstore.AnonStore` binding becomes dead/unsatisfiable for any other consumer.

Device tagging moved onto the synchronous authentication path

`TagDevice` was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout; it is now called inline during `Authenticate`. Every anonymous request whose device ID is not in the 29-minute local cache now performs a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device` (when a limit is configured) plus an upsert before the response can proceed, adding database round-trips to request latency. With randomly generated device IDs (cache misses on every request) this turns each anonymous request into at least two synchronous DB statements, which is a cheap amplification vector against the database. Consider keeping the write asynchronous and only performing the limit check synchronously, or caching the count.

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a second, new device is rejected. There is no test that an *existing* device can still be refreshed once the limit is reached (the main purpose of `updateDevice`), no test that a device whose `updated_at` is older than the 30-day window behaves as intended, and no test of the service-level behaviour (the local-cache interaction in `tagDeviceUI`, which currently lets rejected devices through on subsequent requests). These are the cases most likely to regress.

anonymousDeviceLimit is typed as `undefined` on the boot config and can never actually be undefined

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the property type as `undefined` on `GrafanaBootConfig`; any consumer writing `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0` will fail to type-check even though the value is a number at runtime. Additionally the backend DTO field is a non-pointer `int64` with no `omitempty`, so the frontend always receives a number (0 when no limit is configured) and the declared `number | undefined` in `GrafanaConfig` is misleading. Annotate the field (`anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`) or make the type `number` to match what the server actually sends.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`@loaded_locales ||= []` in ensure_loaded! runs outside LOAD_MUTEX and can discard loaded-locale state

`ensure_loaded!` initializes `@loaded_locales ||= []` without holding `LOAD_MUTEX`, while `load_locale` mutates the same array under the mutex. Two threads racing after a `reload!`/boot can both observe nil and each assign a fresh array, so one thread's `@loaded_locales << locale` is lost and that locale is considered unloaded (causing redundant reloads) or, worse, a partially loaded array is published. The nil-initialization should be done inside the mutex (or at load time of the patch) so all access to `@loaded_locales` is synchronized.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: @loaded_locales is lazily initialized and accessed by concurrent threads without synchronization. The candidate details the specific race (@loaded_locales ||= [] outside LOAD_MUTEX vs. mutation under the mutex) that the golden comment describes.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded in the controller path, so fallbacks silently fail elsewhere

Translations are loaded lazily per locale (`load_locale`), and `translate` only guarantees that `config.locale` is loaded. The new fallback chain (`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]`) is only pre-loaded by `ApplicationController#set_locale` via `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`. Any translation performed outside a web request — Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console, model/service code that sets `I18n.locale` itself — will have the fallback locales' YAML files unloaded, so a missing key in the current locale will not fall back and will return "translation missing" instead. The loading of the fallback chain should happen inside `translate`/`load_locale` (or in `I18n.locale=`) rather than in one before_filter.

LRU translation cache key does not account for the fallback chain (multisite/stale results)

The cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. With fallbacks enabled, the resolved value for a key now also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which is per-site and mutable. In a multisite process the backend is shared, so a value resolved through site A's default-locale fallback will be served from the cache to site B requesting the same key and locale. Likewise, changing `default_locale` on a site does not invalidate the cache, so previously cached fallback results stay stale until a reload. The cache key must include the fallback chain (or the cache must be flushed when `default_locale` changes).

`SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` raises if the setting is nil, and `compact` cannot save it

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` calls `to_sym` on the setting before the array is compacted. If `SiteSetting.default_locale` ever returns nil/blank (unset setting, or SiteSetting not usable yet), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'to_sym' for nil`, from inside every fallback lookup — i.e. from any missing-translation lookup. Guard with something like `SiteSetting.default_locale.presence&.to_sym` so the intended `compact` actually works.

Fallback chain is recomputed (with a SiteSetting read) on every lookup and may run before the DB is available

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` ignores the Hash storage and recomputes the chain on every call, including a `SiteSetting.default_locale` read and a fresh array allocation. `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` normally memoizes the computed chain; here every translation miss hits SiteSetting and allocates. More importantly, this code can be invoked in contexts where SiteSetting/DB is not available (asset precompilation, migrations, boot-time translations), where it will raise instead of returning a usable chain. Consider memoizing per locale and keying/invalidating on `default_locale`, and rescuing to `[locale, :en]` when SiteSetting is unavailable.

No specs cover the new server-side fallback behaviour

This change introduces a custom fallback chain (user locale → site default locale → :en) plus on-demand loading of all fallback locales, replacing the `config.i18n.fallbacks = true` environment settings. There are no tests asserting that a key missing in the user locale resolves from the site default locale and then from English, that the fallback locales get loaded by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, or that changing `SiteSetting.default_locale` takes effect. Given the lazy-loading and LRU caching interactions in `translate_accelerator`, these paths are easy to break silently (missing translations will now be masked rather than raised).

A mutating endpoint should require a POST/PUT (or a one-time signed key as the digest unsubscribe does), with the GET URL only rendering a confirmation page.

The Ember `topicUnsubscribe` route only loads the topic view; the actual notification-level change happens server-side in `TopicsController#unsubscribe` during the initial HTML request. Any client-side transition to `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` (an in-app link, or browser back/forward handled by the SPA without a full page load) will render "You will stop receiving notifications for …" while nothing was changed on the server, misleading the user. `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` always says "You will stop receiving notifications for <title>", but the server toggles: a user at `watching`/`tracking` is moved to `regular` (which still emails on replies to their posts, mentions and quotes) and only a second click sets `muted`. The untested branches include: missing `TopicUser` row (currently a 500), the watching→regular vs regular→muted toggle, the slug-mismatch 301 redirect, the not-logged-in path, and that the JSON/HTML responses render. false_positives.candidate:
Credential-sync request is unauthenticated and its status is never checked

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret/signature header (unlike the inbound webhook, which verifies `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), so the self-hoster's endpoint has no way to tell that the request really came from Cal.com — anybody who knows the URL can harvest access tokens for arbitrary user ids if the endpoint trusts the caller. In addition the response status is never checked, so a 4xx/5xx body is passed to the token parsers as if it were a token response, producing confusing downstream failures instead of a clear error.

`prisma` is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService

The newly added code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` inside `getClient`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile error (and a `ReferenceError` at runtime if type-checking is bypassed), so every Salesforce booking/calendar operation fails as soon as the service is instantiated.

Salesforce token is refreshed unconditionally on every service instantiation

`getClient` issues a refresh_token request to `login.salesforce.com` and a `credential.update` write every time a `SalesforceCalendarService` is constructed, with no expiry check on the stored token. Since the service is constructed per booking/availability operation this adds a blocking round trip plus a DB write to every request and will hit Salesforce's refresh-token rate limits on busy instances.

Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo", which is not the app's slug

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug used everywhere else (callback stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint looks the app up with `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`) is `zoom`. A self-hoster keying off `appSlug` will not be able to map the sync request back to the credential the webhook created, so Zoom credential syncing silently fails.

Webex refresh still validated with the strict provider schema, so credential sync cannot work

Webex was switched to `refreshOAuthTokens` but the response is still validated with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(...)`, which requires an exact `scope` literal, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. A self-hosted sync endpoint is documented to return only the access token and expiry, so the parse always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here (as done for zoom/office365) or don't wire Webex into the sync flow.

Updating synced credentials does not clear the `invalid` flag

When a credential already exists the handler only writes `key`. Credentials that were previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. google/zoom/webex set this on `invalid_grant`) stay invalid after fresh keys are pushed in, so Cal.com keeps treating the connection as broken even though valid tokens were just synced. The update should also reset `invalid: false`.

Webhook secret compared with a non-constant-time `!==` and header may be an array

The shared secret check uses a plain string inequality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is therefore vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally `req.headers[name]` can be `string[]` when the header is sent twice, in which case the comparison always fails and legitimate callers get a 403 with no explanation.

findFirst + update can leave duplicate credentials out of sync

Because the lookup is `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })`, when a user has more than one credential row for the same app (which happens for several apps that historically allowed duplicates) only one row is updated; the stale rows keep their old keys and may still be selected by other code paths (`findFirst` is used in several adapters). Two concurrent webhook deliveries can also both see no credential and create two rows. Consider a unique constraint or an `updateMany`/transaction.

No tests for the new credential webhook or the token-parsing helpers

This PR adds a publicly reachable endpoint that decrypts a payload and writes third-party OAuth credentials for arbitrary user ids, plus two new shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) used by ~10 app integrations, with no unit tests. Basic tests covering secret mismatch, unknown user/app, bad ciphertext, create-vs-update behaviour, and the token-schema fallback would have caught the schema and response-shape defects noted elsewhere in this review.

On a serverless runtime the function can be frozen/terminated right after the response, so the flag is never written and the cron job will never cancel the scheduled SendGrid email — the reminder for a cancelled booking is still delivered. false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid cancellation aborts the whole cancellation loop permanently

The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop is wrapped in a single outer `try`/`catch`. If the `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` request throws for one reminder (invalid/expired batch id, already-cancelled batch, transient 4xx/5xx), the catch is hit, the loop aborts, and none of the remaining reminders in the batch are cancelled; the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected so far are never awaited either (Prisma promises are lazy), so nothing is removed from the DB. Because the next cron run re-selects the same rows ordered the same way, a single permanently-failing reminder blocks every other cancellation forever and reminder emails for cancelled/rescheduled bookings keep going out — exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. The try/catch (and the delete) should be inside the loop, per reminder.

Deferred cancellation can miss SendGrid's cancellation deadline for near-term reminders

Cancellation is deferred to a cron that runs every ~15 minutes and only picks up reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour. A booking cancelled shortly before its reminder's send time (e.g. 12 minutes before) will only have the SendGrid cancel request issued on the next cron tick, which can be less than SendGrid's required 10-minute lead time before `sendAt` — in that case the cancel is rejected/ignored and the reminder email is still sent. Worse, the `deleteMany` at line 34 removes EMAIL reminders whose `scheduledDate` is already in the past before the cancellation block runs, so such rows are dropped without any cancellation attempt and without any log. Consider cancelling immediately when `scheduledDate` is near (while keeping the deferred path for far-future reminders) so the pending-cancellation quota is still protected.

Unused `Prisma` import left behind after removing BatchPayload usage

The import block was changed from `import type { Prisma, PrismaPromise }` to a value import that still includes `Prisma`, but all `Prisma.BatchPayload` usages were removed in this diff, so `Prisma` is now unused in this file. With the repo's no-unused-vars/consistent-type-imports lint rules this fails CI; the formatting of the new import block (no trailing comma on the last specifier) will also be flagged by the prettier check.

Cancellation query does not restrict to EMAIL reminders with a reference id

`remindersToCancel` selects every `workflowReminder` with `cancelled: true`, without filtering on `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`, `scheduled: true` or `referenceId: { not: null }`. Today only email reminders are ever flagged, but any future/manual row with another method (or a null `referenceId`) would be POSTed to SendGrid as a `batch_id`, producing an error that — given the shared try/catch — aborts the whole cancellation loop. Add the explicit filters so this endpoint only ever handles rows it can act on.

No automated coverage for the cancelled-reminder flow

This is the second attempt at fixing reminders being sent for cancelled/rescheduled bookings (the previous fix in #6991 silently stopped working in production). The PR adds a new `cancelled` field plus a new cron branch but no test asserting that cancelling or rescheduling a booking marks the reminder `cancelled: true`, that the cron issues the SendGrid cancel and removes the row, and that a failing cancellation does not block the others. Without a test the regression can recur unnoticed, as it already did.

false_positives.candidate:
EventManager built from the caller's credentials, not the booking organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` fetches the credentials of the logged-in caller, and the EventManager is constructed with `{...user, credentials}`. Since this endpoint is reachable by attendees and team admins (not just the organizer), the calendar/video update in `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` will be attempted with credentials that do not own the external calendar event, so the attendee update silently fails (or targets the wrong account). No validation of booking status or time before adding guests

The handler accepts any `bookingId` and never checks `booking.status` or whether the booking is in the past. The UI only exposes the action for upcoming/confirmed bookings, but the tRPC mutation is directly callable, so guests can be added to CANCELLED/REJECTED or long-past bookings, which then triggers confirmation/ics emails for an event that no longer exists. It also does not account for `seatsPerTimeSlot`: adding attendees to a seated event bypasses the seat limit and creates attendees with no seat reference.

`sendAddGuestsEmails` loops over `calendarEvent.team?.members` to notify co-hosts, but the `evt` built in `addGuests.handler.ts` never populates `team` (the booking query selects `eventType` without team/hosts). For team events, only the primary organizer is emailed and the branch is dead code.

`name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw a TypeError if `calEvent.attendees` is empty, which would reject the whole `sendAddGuestsEmails` promise chain. Other organizer templates guard this; use optional access or fall back to the organizer/team name.

Email failure swallowed without the error details

`catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` discards `err`, so a mail delivery or template failure leaves no diagnosable trace. Use the project `logger` and include `safeStringify(err)` plus the booking id.

Invalid-email banner is never cleared and empty submit is a silent no-op

`setIsInvalidEmail(false)` is only called by the Cancel button; on a successful mutation (or when the user corrects the input) the flag stays true, so the red "Emails must be unique and valid" message is still displayed the next time the dialog is opened via the dropdown. `packages/ui/form/MultiEmail.tsx` imports `Button, EmailField, Icon, Tooltip` from `@calcom/ui`, while `packages/ui/index.tsx` re-exports this very module (via `MultiEmailLazy`). The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that writes attendees and sends emails, with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer / attendee / team admin), blacklist filtering and duplicate filtering, but no unit or integration tests were added. Regressions in the permission branches would silently allow or deny guest additions; the AND/OR bug in the team check is exactly the kind of defect a test would have caught.
